📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know.
  • Like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules.
  • However, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know. (Photo: Challenge Family).

Like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules. For example, you’re not allowed to cut the course, have a motor on your bike, curse at officials, punch a rival, or, most craven of all, have fewer than three safety pins on your race number in France.

However, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of. Some of them, we’ve helpfully outlined below:.

2. Forever Alone — The training paradox. The more you do triathlons, the more all your friends are triathletes, and the more you will train alone.

Recent findings suggest that 3. You Are Not Kristian — The Norwegian Method is to train more hours in a day than you do not train. For more training methods, see YouTube.

According to recent reports, 4. The Devil’s in the Details — Dedicate 20 hours a week to training for three months in the lead up to your A race. Spend zero minutes working on transition.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Shelve Twitter Hate — Write a mantra on your water bottle and start an Instagram account for reels, stories, and collabs. Don’t be an angry person on Twitter. That’s not cool.

Recent findings suggest that 6. Match at All Costs — Never sacrifice style for performance. Color-coded kit and equipment are essential, unless you’re going for garish retro, which is an acceptable look for 2026 only.

7. Weather or Not? — Check the weather forecast and water temperature before checking the weather forecast and water temperature, and then solicit opinions on what the weather and water temperature are likely to be on race day.

According to recent reports, 8. Wetsuit Your Worries Away — Convince yourself you can’t swim without a wetsuit/won’t be able to get your wetsuit off if it’s a wetsuit swim.

9. Experience Equals Complacency — The athlete guide must be studied with a focus that inversely correlates to how many races the athlete has done.

It has been revealed that 10. Selfie First, Reality Later — Take a selfie with the giant M-Dot “Ironman Is In Town” sign. Post this to social media as soon as you land, feigning a smile because although you’ve arrived, your bike hasn’t yet followed.

Sources indicate that 11. Hell’s Bells — Set three alarms minimum and then wonder why the first of them is going off as you force-feed yourself rice because you couldn’t sleep anyway.

In a recent development, 12. Nothing Matters as Much as Everything — Take time to stare at your race tattoo, realize the transfer has only half stuck, and have a mild panic by convincing yourself you’ll be disqualified before the start.

Industry observers note that 13. Apply Liberally — Use sunscreen, making sure you miss a key patch of skin. It will show more of your suffering.

In a recent development, 14. Pay it Forward — In the name of karma, offer to: a) Zip up someone’s wetsuit; b) Lend them a bike pump (even if it’s not yours); c) Thank everyone you see profusely and wish them all a great day.

Industry observers note that 15. Ride the Intake Earthquake — Increase your volume of carbohydrates per hour exponentially with the same dedication you had when you raced 15 years ago and were insistent on using only your 5% body fat as a fuel source.

In a recent development, 16. Be a Bathroom Banterer — Talk with bravado about your trained ability to both pee in the swim and on the bike while you stand for an hour in a revolving porta potty line.

17. What’s Good for the Goose is Good for the Gander — Oops! You punched someone in the eye in the swim completely by accident. Also, the breaststroker you got stuck behind at the first buoy deliberately kicked you in the face.

According to recent reports, 18. Meditate on Aquatic Paradoxes — During the swim, reflect on: a) Whoever learned to swim as a kid is basically a cheater. Or b) “Why do triathletes swim so freaking slowly?”.

19. Style Reigns — Replace existing drink bottles on the bike with those from the on-course sponsor. Call bottles bidons if you’ve ever watched a clip of the Tour de France.

20. The Refs Need You (Really) — Become militant about drafting and shout obscenities at a pack who: a). Aren’t in the race anyway; b) Are out for a gentle social weekend ride; c) Are still moving faster than you.

21. Ride the Highs and Lows — When you are riding downhill, you think you will win. When you are riding uphill, you think you will come last.

22. Roll the Dice — Breathe a sigh of relief when you complete the bike leg without puncturing because you haven’t practiced changing tires for five years.

23. Don’t be Patronizing Pat — If you pass someone on the run, resist the urge to tap them encouragingly on the back. One athlete’s chirpy come-on is another athlete’s patronizing pat. And if you must do it, always avoid the backside.

It has been revealed that 24. Leave Self-Awareness Back at the Hotel — Do something in the finish chute that in any other walk of life you would find cringey. This includes sweaty mess marriage proposals to a long-suffering partner who has a cooked neck from staring at a race tracker for the past 14 hours.

25. Be Congratulating Carl — Always congratulate the first person you see at the finish. However hollow-eyed your expression or soiled your tri suit. It’s your duty to have that mutual moment with a complete stranger.

26. The Rules of Race Photography are Unbending — Acknowledge that official race photographs only ever capture: 1. Grotesque faces. 2: When you “briefly” sat up out of aero. 3. Ugly heel strikes.

Industry observers note that 27. You’re the Best — Use multiple filters of the race results, including but not limited to age-groups, disciplines (including transitions), and nationalities to claim a top-10 position at some aspect of your race. If you rode a road bike, you can also disqualify everyone who rode a TT/tri bike.

In a recent development, 28. Brutality Reigns — Include the word “brutal” at least three times during any social media race report.

Who’s ready for coaching? 7 GLP-1 clients, from “not yet” to “let’s go!”

📅 11 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that reviewed by Brian St.
  • That’s the thought many health and fitness coaches had when GLP-1 medications first hit the mass market.
  • Recent findings suggest that though semaglutide (Ozempic) became available in 2017, it initially felt like a theoretical threat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that reviewed by Brian St. Pierre, MS, RD.

That’s the thought many health and fitness coaches had when GLP-1 medications first hit the mass market.

Recent findings suggest that though semaglutide (Ozempic) became available in 2017, it initially felt like a theoretical threat. Prescription rates were still very low, and it seemed like no one actually knew anyone who was taking it.

Now, in 2026, over 1 in 10 US adults are taking a GLP-1 medication. Most of us know someone on it (or we’re on it ourselves).

In a recent development, with wider use, opinions towards the medication have softened too. Most coaches no longer see it as a threat, and instead appreciate it as a valuable tool for certain clients, with coaching as an additive complement.

Recent findings suggest that many coaches still have concerns though, primarily about their clients’ long term health on the medication. (Among the worries: Loss of muscle mass! Using a “band-aid” solution! Bypassing foundational health habits! And more!).

However, whether you count yourself as a GLP-1 supporter or a GLP-1 skeptic, there’s a framing that might change the way you think about your work in this field:.

As Kate Solovieva, Super Coach and PN’s Director of Community, notes: “As a coach, you’re not in the GLP-1 world; you’re in the GLP-1 support world.”.

It has been revealed that that’s actually good news. Because trying to coach everyone taking a GLP-1 just isn’t possible. And spending time thinking about all the people using GLP-1s “the wrong way” is, bluntly, wasted energy. Some of those people just don’t want, need, or aren’t ready for your help.

Meanwhile, there is a subgroup of people on GLP-1s who are ready, willing, and able to receive your support. Honing in on this group is where you can actually make a difference (and where your business can thrive).

Recent findings suggest that in the following article, we’ll cover seven GLP-1 clients you’re likely to meet. Each reflects a different point in the GLP-1 medication journey, and a different level of readiness for coaching. Based on our experience coaching over 175,000 clients (of which an increasing number are on GLP-1s), we’ll offer strategies to work with each.

Before we begin, a reminder: People change, and readiness isn’t fixed.

A person who starts off saying “I’m doing fine on my own” may eventually morph into “I’m flailing and really need someone else in my corner”—and vice versa.

If the person in front of you sounds like one of these clients, that’s where they are right now. So listen carefully to how your client speaks at every session, and respond dynamically.

In general, Coach Kate says someone is usually ready for coaching when they demonstrate two things:.

Keep that in the back of your mind as you interact with client prospects, and as you read about each client, summarized in the table below.

Now, on to the different GLP-1 clients.

This is the person who’s started a GLP-1 medication—and they love it.

They’ve experienced minimal side effects, and have gotten great results on a relatively low dose.

They haven’t changed much about their exercise habits or their diet (except the eating less part, which the medication has taken care of), but they’re seeing what they want to see on the scale, so they don’t feel motivated to change anything.

It might be tempting to “lure” this kind of client in by warning them of the dangers of using a GLP-1 medication without adding in long-term health behaviors (like resistance training and strategic nutrition), but this type of approach can backfire.

At best, you may sound like a downer. At worst, you may sound like an active antagonist.

Industry observers note that in Motivational Interviewing, a communication approach commonly used in coaching, this is called the “righting reflex.” It’s the urge that coaches, counselors, and therapists often have to help or “correct course” for their client. You see them doing something “wrong,” and you want to help them “fix” it.

However, following this instinct may actually strengthen a client’s defenses, and prevent change.

If a person is flying high on their current approach, their readiness for coaching is extremely low.

As Coach Kate says, “they’re just not my person yet.”.

Your best move with this client is to genuinely celebrate their current results, then plant the seed for support should they need it in the future.

For example, you could say: “It must feel so good to see all these positive results! If you ever feel like you want to work on another layer, like resistance training or optimizing your nutrition, I’d love to work together.”.

In a recent development, then, just stay available. (“My door is always open!”).

This is the person who hasn’t started a GLP-1 medication—and might never, despite being a great candidate for one.

Maybe their doctor has already suggested the medication to them and they’ve read everything they can on the topic.

Sources indicate that and yet, they’re frozen with fear at the starting line. They’re afraid of side effects, of being on medication for life, of not holding up their end of the bargain. (“I’ve been trying to start strength training for years. If I take this medication it matters even more… What if I still can’t do it?”).

In a recent development, toni Bauer, Super Coach and PN’s Director of Coaching and Education Operations also says that, in some cases, a client’s hesitation isn’t about side effects. “Some of our clients wonder, ‘Am I a good person or a bad person if I start taking a GLP-1 medication? Am I weak? Am I giving up?’” Coach Toni says these concerns aren’t unique to GLP-1 medications, but they seem to be especially common.

She reasons, “If you have high cholesterol, are you weak for taking cholesterol medication? No. But often people don’t view obesity as a disease at a societal level, so the conversation is different here.”.

Regardless of the root cause of this person’s hesitation, the advice below can help them find clarity.

According to recent reports, first, let’s be clear: Deciding whether or not to take a medication isn’t a coaching decision, and falls out of your scope of practice. That choice is ultimately up to your client and a medical provider who can assess whether a GLP-1 is appropriate given their medical history.

That noted, clients may still come to you wanting to discuss their options.

So the question becomes: How do you support someone through a decision you can’t make for them?

Recent findings suggest that coach Toni advises: “You can share facts and data. For example, study results and what you’ve seen with other clients. But you can’t say, ‘For you, this is the right choice.’”.

Instead, the biggest coaching opportunity here is to help clients articulate what’s actually driving their hesitation.

This hesitation about whether to do something different or stay the same is called ambivalence, and it’s a normal (albeit uncomfortable) stage of change.

Problem is, without the right tools, a person can stay stuck in ambivalence for months or even years. And, much like being stuck at an airport in between two destinations, it sucks.

But at PN, we have a cool exercise to deal with client ambivalence. It’s called the 4 Crazy Questions. Essentially, you explore:.

In this context, the questions can help a client explore the risk of starting a GLP-1 (which they’ve probably already voiced), but also the risk of not starting, which they may not have considered yet.

Our 4 Crazy Questions worksheet can encourage clients to explore the pros and cons of both choices. With these considerations laid out explicitly, most people feel a lot more clear about their next steps—or at least what questions they need to ask their medical provider before they can move forward.

Importantly, this exercise doesn’t have a “right” outcome. Some people work through it and fill the prescription. Others decide the medication isn’t for them, and that’s fine. (It’s also worth reminding clients that starting isn’t necessarily permanent: With their provider’s input, a trial run on the medication is a perfectly valid way in.).

Either way, there are opportunities to support your client. As Coach Toni puts it: “Whether you go ‘natural’ or whether you go GLP-1, the foundational habits are essentially the same.”.

This is the person who started a GLP-1 with lots of optimism—and now feels like they have a plague that won’t end.

In a cruel twist, this person might actually be seeing great fat loss results. And yet, they’re nauseated, exhausted, dreading their next dose, and wondering whether it’s worth continuing this medication.

It has been revealed that adding to their sense of defeat, they may also be comparing themselves to a “Honeymooner” in their life, so they might also be wondering if there’s something wrong with them. (“It worked so well for my friend! I must be broken in some way.”).

First, offer some neutral education to depersonalize their experience.

Namely, they should know that side effects are extremely common: About half of customers report nausea, a third report diarrhea, and a fifth report vomiting.1 So, what this person thinks is exceptional might actually just be a normal adjustment. (This doesn’t make the experience suck less, but it can give them some hope.).

Also, getting GLP-1s right is a process of trial and error: the right medication, the right dose, and the right nutritional strategies to reduce symptoms.

Sources indicate that if their symptoms are severe, get them to loop in their doctor. Medication type and dosing is under the purview of a medical professional, so involving them is essential.

After that, your best coaching move is to suggest an experiment.

Recent findings suggest that ▶ Ask about dose. To be clear, you’re asking about it, not adjusting it. Says Coach Toni: “Often, when people are experiencing extreme side effects, they’ve ratcheted up their dose too rapidly. Sometimes the easiest way to keep somebody on a GLP-1 who’s experiencing high side effects is to lower their dosage.” Coach Toni makes clear that while dosage isn’t a coach’s domain, you can help draw a client’s attention to it.

Industry observers note that ▶ Start a food journal. It doesn’t need to be every day—just around the meals that precede the worst symptoms. You’re looking for three things:.

▶ Try smaller portions, eaten more often. Coach Toni notes if you only try one thing, this one is the most reliable strategy. GLP-1 clients may be tempted to cut meals when symptoms are high, but this increases the likelihood of undereating and nutrient deficiencies. The goal, in her words: “Can we get small enough, frequent enough meals that we get nutrients in, but they never feel overwhelmed or super full?”.

To stay within your scope of practice, language matters.

Don’t say: “You’re nauseous, so you should eat smaller meals.”.

In a recent development, instead, say: “Folks who are nauseous sometimes do better with smaller, more frequent meals. Want to try it this week and see what you notice?”.

In the first example, you’ve offered a “prescription” (which coaches can’t legally do). In the second example, you’ve offered an experiment to consider.

Side effects (such as nausea, vomiting, constipation, and/or diarrhea) are extremely common among GLP-1 customers, and typically last one to two weeks after initiating the medication. Some symptoms can last longer (particularly constipation), but most are mild to moderate, and usually improve within a few weeks.

Recent findings suggest that symptoms can also return each time a dosage is increased, though they’re usually milder and more short-lived. These too tend to improve after the first week or so.

However, you should strongly encourage a client to reach out promptly to their medical provider if they notice:.

Reassure your client they’re not being dramatic by reporting these symptoms. Their medical team needs to hear this kind of information to help them get the best results, while preserving overall health.

Industry observers note that also: Your client will get better care if they show up prepared. So, get them to jot down and bring:.

This is the person whose results look great, but less visible changes are creating longer term risks.

Sources indicate that this person is likely to be quite sedentary, and when you ask what they do for exercise, they might tell you “I walk.” But they’re not the outlier kind of walker who consistently gets 20,000 steps a day. They just… walk a little.

Women are more likely to fall into this category, especially if they come from a generation or culture where strength training simply wasn’t a thing women did (or were welcomed to do).

Additionally, this person might be running on a decades-long plain-toast-and-coffee breakfast habit, with lower protein intake already ingrained before medication further reduced appetite.

Sources indicate that the scale is dropping though, so they’re thrilled. It’s just that nobody’s measuring what kind of weight is dropping.

According to recent reports, keep in mind that this description is a starting hypothesis, not a diagnosis. Low activity and low protein raise the risk of muscle loss, but they don’t confirm it. That’s what the measures below are for.

Industry observers note that your job is to bring awareness to the invisible. Because once this person sees what’s at stake, they’ll be more likely to see the value in changing their habits, and in coaching.

However, theoretical warnings about muscle loss are easy to dismiss.

This is one of the reasons why Coach Kate states, “I don’t care if I coach you or not—please just get a DEXA as a baseline.”.

When a person has a quantifiable, objective measure of their muscle composition, it’s often more motivating than any amount of abstract concern.

Ideally, every person who begins a GLP-1 medication should get a DEXA scan before they start, then again at six or twelve months to see how they’re progressing.

According to recent reports, if a client can’t or won’t do a DEXA, assess strength and function in other ways. Ask: “How do the stairs feel compared to a few months ago? What about carrying groceries?” Gather objective data too, recording baselines for squat, deadlift, and bench press (or other accessible exercises) to compare to over time. Declines in any of these areas can reveal potential muscle loss, and can motivate a client to take action.

Without protective strategies, up to 40 percent of weight lost from GLP-1 medications can come from lean mass, with a majority of that being muscle.2.

In order to prevent that from happening, there are two behaviors to prioritize:.

Industry observers note that ▶ Protein at every meal. When appetite is suppressed, every bite has to earn its place. Aim for 25-40 grams of protein at every meal and 15-20 grams for snacks. (On days when appetite is severely suppressed, protein powders can be a more palatable way to reach that target.).

It has been revealed that ▶ Strength training, scaled to what they’d actually do. The term “weight lifting” might overwhelm a person who’s never set foot in a gym, so don’t start there. Start where PN always starts: Ask what they could do twice this week that they’re 9-out-of-10 confident they’d actually do. Sit-to-stands off the couch. A few moves with a resistance band. Bodyweight anything. Scale up from there, one week at a time.

This is the person for whom the medication has worked a little too well.

Their appetite hasn’t just decreased—it’s gone.

Industry observers note that they’re not eating enough, and often don’t notice until you ask. “When did you last eat?” you say, and they say, “Ummm… Yesterday afternoon? I think?”.

Their protein and overall calorie intake is plummeting, and soon their energy levels will too.

Plus, something more subtle might also be happening: Food stops being a pleasure and becomes a chore, or even a source of dread.

Sources indicate that for some, this might seem like an upside down world. They may have spent their whole life fighting to eat less. The idea of fighting to eat more feels completely absurd—and entirely off their radar.

Before anything else: If there’s an active eating disorder in the picture, this medication likely shouldn’t have been prescribed. A vulnerability to disordered eating can both contribute to or be triggered by the above scenario.

Sources indicate that so, scope of practice first. Ask this person if they’ve ever struggled with disordered eating. If the answer is yes, refer out to a doctor or a dietitian. You can absolutely stay involved as a guide, but not as the only professional in the room. Have your referral network ready before you need it.

Recent findings suggest that but sometimes, you won’t know. Your client may have been screened and cleared. Or, they may not have disclosed. So your job is to figure out what you’re actually looking at—and that starts with what Coach Toni calls the “show me” approach.

Industry observers note that as with every client here, treat this one as something to investigate, not a label. Rather than acting on a hunch, collect something concrete, such as a few days of food logging (in writing or via photos).

From there, it branches two ways.

Industry observers note that ▶ If they’ll track, do some food math, and the numbers may do the work for you. When some clients see that their calorie intake is hovering around 800 to 1,000 Calories per day, it’s the only wake up call they need. They weren’t intentionally restricting; they genuinely just had no idea.

For this client, establishing an eating routine is the best next action.

It has been revealed that your client may be used to following appetite as a cue to eat, but now that medication has removed it, they need a different cue. That means eating on a schedule, likely every 3–4 hours, including protein at every one of those occasions. Portions can be small if appetite is very low, but they should be nutrient-dense.

▶ If they won’t track—and especially if they resist in a way that feels purposely avoidant—that resistance itself is information.

Coach Toni suggests that if you suspect that disordered eating is in the picture and a client is really resistant about tracking, it might be time for a crucial conversation—an often uncomfortable, but honest and essential conversation between a client and a coach.

She suggests leading with non-judgement and safety. For example:.

“I want you to know this is a safe space to talk. My goal as a coach is always to prioritize your overall health. However, there have been a couple of things you’ve shared recently that have me wondering whether we’re protecting your body’s basic needs.”.

Sources indicate that then name the specific things you noticed, sticking to facts. (“You’ve mentioned you’ve been losing hair and struggling more during workouts. Those can both be signs of undereating. Would you be open to revisiting food journaling for a short stretch so we can see more clearly what’s happening, or telling your doctor about your symptoms?”).

If this conversation is enough to help a client see the value in tracking, follow the advice after “If they’ll track” above.

If what surfaces is a genuinely troubled relationship with food, refer out, while offering to stay involved for support as needed.

This is the person who got the results they wanted with the medication, and is now choosing to wean off.

They’re not quitting because of crappy results or intolerable side effects, they’ve simply decided they don’t want to be on a GLP-1 forever.

The coaching opportunity here is, in part, about tempering expectations.

Sources indicate that most people imagine coming off as the finish line. Instead though, it’s more like starting a different endurance course: The medication has been managing their appetite, and now they have to.

Industry observers note that ideally, you start working with this client while the medication is still doing some of the heavy lifting with appetite regulation. If you can have six months to build the right habits as well as prepare mentally for the tapering off period, your client will be in a much better position.

Make sure the previously mentioned habits—like resistance training and optimizing protein—are already firmly established. If your client is managing those habits consistently (not perfectly, but consistently), even on their busiest, most stressful, most side-effect-disrupted days, then they’re more likely to be able to maintain them when they’re off their medication and food distractions re-enter the picture.

After that, work on how you’ll continue to define success. This client has been accustomed to measuring it on the scale, but the scale will move—some regain is normal. So, ask them early: What does success look like if the scale ticks up eight pounds but your habits hold?

Sources indicate that be honest about the odds, too. People who changed nothing while on the medication almost universally regain most of the weight—usually within the first year and a half or so3—because the appetite that went down comes right back up.

However, people who integrate and sustain healthier nutrition and exercise behaviors while they’re on medication are four times better at maintaining a ten percent or higher weight loss when they come off the medication.4.

This is the person who was also getting great results on the medication—except instead of choosing to go off it on their own time, they’re forced to quit due to external circumstances.

Maybe their insurance stopped covering it, or they lost the job that came with the benefits, or the one drug they tolerated turned out to cost four times as much as the one they couldn’t tolerate.

About 50 percent of GLP-1 owners stop the medication within the first year of using it.5 Some stop due to side effects, and others stop because they’ve gotten the results they want and they want to see if they can maintain them drug-free. But many are simply priced out. The latter is an especially frustrating scenario because, for this person, a “solution” exists. It’s just that, for them, the solution is out of reach.

Understandably, this person may be angry or even ashamed that they can’t afford this medication. Those feelings may or may not show up in your coaching, but it’s good to prepare for them anyway.

First, reassure this person that this is a system failure, not a personal one.

Whether someone can access affordable medication comes down to their insurance blueprint, the region they live in, and their socioeconomic status—also known as the social determinants of health. Those forces shape health outcomes far more than willpower does, and none of them are a measure of how hard someone has tried or how “worthy” they are.

Acknowledging that reality isn’t about throwing up your hands and saying, “Well, I’m screwed!” Rather, it’s about accepting some miserable truths about the world, and then shifting from self-blame to problem-solving.

Once they’ve had a chance to process some (very valid) anger and disappointment, it’s time to focus on what they can control.

Recent findings suggest that at PN, we call this the Spheres of Control exercise. The image below shows you how it works.

Access, price, and coverage are not on the list of controllables, and fighting those realities may only compound frustration.

Meanwhile, they can control other influential factors, like their protein intake, their training, their sleep, their food environment, and maybe their next insurance appeal.

Use the image above to begin a conversation with your client about what is within their control, and lean in hard on those factors.

The truth is, you can’t predict how a client will respond to medication. And, some regain after stopping it is expected.

However, diet and lifestyle habits hugely affect what kind of weight clients lose, plus the rate and amount of that regain.

It has been revealed that “I can’t promise anyone they’ll lose a specific amount of weight or that they’ll never regain it—and I’d be suspicious of any coach who did. What I can tell you is that the habits we build while the medication is doing its work are the ones that’ll still stand when it isn’t.”.

According to recent reports, of course, “coming off” isn’t the endpoint for everyone. Many providers now treat obesity as a chronic condition and these medications as long-term therapy—the same way we’d treat cardiac disease. Again, whether someone stays on, tapers, or stops is a conversation for them and their provider.

Recent findings suggest that but for those who do come off, Coach Toni claims the people who hold their results share one thing: “They maintain consistency with their behaviors as if they were still on the medication. Like nothing changes.”.

She shares an analogy for why that works:.

Sources indicate that “Think about the Oregon Trail. Wagon wheels made ruts in the trail by hitting the same ground over and over and over. You can still see those ruts today. Habits are the same way: If you lay down those neural pathways and reinforce them enough times while your client is on the medication, they’ll have a better chance of continuing on the same path even when they go off the medication.”.

It’s not: “You’ll keep it off.”.

It’s: “While the medication is doing its work, we’ll cut ruts deep enough that those pathways will still be there after the medication is gone.”.

Practically, that means regular resistance training, rock solid nutrition, appetite awareness, and attending to the parts of health that never show up on a scale—sleep, energy, mood, relationships, and identity, which is where Coach Toni lands:.

According to recent reports, “Ideally, your client will have embraced the identity of a ‘upcoming person.’ As in, ‘I am the person who wakes up at 6 a.m. and walks two miles. I am the person who eats protein at every meal. I am the person who does resistance training because it builds the tissue I need to age well.’ That’s the client who maintains.”.

The seven client examples above help you answer two questions:.

Is this person ready for coaching?

How do I meet them where they are?

Once someone becomes your client, the question changes to:.

And when nausea, fatigue, stalled results, and weakening strength and physical function all show up at once in the same client, that can be tricky to answer.

Knowing where to start is one of the core skills taught in the upcoming GLP Coaching Institute Certification, developed in partnership with Precision Nutrition.

Industry observers note that the certification combines GLP-1-specific science and practical coaching frameworks with PN’s proven coaching methodology. You’ll learn how to use a framework called The Five GLP-1 Types: Strength, Fuel, Fitness, Recovery, and Results.

Unlike the profiles in this article, the Five Types aren’t about how ready clients are. They’re coaching priorities: a way to decide what to work on first, and when to shift focus as a client’s needs change.

Recent findings suggest that to learn more, join the waitlist. You’ll be the first to know when the certification launches, with early access before enrolment opens to everyone else.

One Bike for Everything? Our Editors Tested Hybrid Bikes for Daily Riding—These 10 Picks Are Best for Commuting, Fitness, and Light Trails

📅 23 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2308 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that when I worked in bike shops, we sold tons of hybrid bikes.
  • Outside of cycling circles, the term “hybrid” often refers to vehicles that pair an electric motor with an internal combustion engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that when I worked in bike shops, we sold tons of hybrid bikes. These bicycles are ideal for riders who say, “I need a bike that does a little of everything.” If you’re seeking versatility, a hybrid is often your best bike option. They’re a good choice for general fitness, commuting, running errands, and family rides.

Outside of cycling circles, the term “hybrid” often refers to vehicles that pair an electric motor with an internal combustion engine. However, in bike-speak, hybrids are a bicycle style that combines elements of road bikes and mountain bikes. Hybrids range from lightweight, sporty bikes designed for roads and bike paths to more rugged models suitable for light off-road use.

Industry observers note that while they’re not ideal for die-hard mountain bikers or roadies seeking speed and the highest performance, hybrids work surprisingly well for many people on real-world rides. Typically, hybrids blend the lightweight frame, fast-rolling tires, and larger gears of road bikes with flat handlebars and the upright riding position of hardtail mountain bikes. Some hybrid models also feature suspension forks similar to those used on bikes designed for more aggressive, technical trails.

In a recent development, the Cannondale Quick 3 is our overall favorite hybrid for its fast feel and smooth ride, comfortable upright riding position, and reasonable price. These qualities make it great for fresh riders who may be hesitant about incorporating regular bike riding into their routine.

The Quick 3 features a comfortable Selle Royal saddle and Ergon grips. It also has mounts for adding a rear rack (the fork lacks rack mounts, however) and fenders to keep road spray out of your eyes and off your backside. While the pricier Quick 2 features a carbon fork and 1x9 Shimano drivetrain, the Quick 3 uses a steel fork and 1x8-speed Shimano system. These differences add a little weight, but the bike still has the gear range to tackle the hills on your commute or rides.

In a recent development, cannondale also offers the Quick 3 with a step-through frame. It also sells the Quick CX 3 model with a suspension fork.

BUY QUICK 3 STEP-THROUGH - $749 BUY QUICK CX 3 - $849.

The CTY 1.1 (by REI’s Co-op Cycles house brand) is a capable, affordable hybrid. The CTY is a great choice for a wide range of riders—especially for budget-minded beginners and commuters. The bike has an upright riding position (versus the sporty fit of fitness-focused hybrids). This geometry, along with a comfortable memory foam saddle and gel grips, makes the CTY 1.1 more comfortable than many competitors.

Commuters will appreciate the CTY’s flat-resistant, wire-bead 40mm tires with reflective sidewalls; they let you roll over potholes, dirt, gravel, random road debris, and even the occasional curb. For all-weather stopping power, REI equips the bike with Tektro mechanical disc brakes, and the Shimano 3x8-speed drivetrain gives you enough gear range to get you most anywhere you want to go.

BUY CTY 1.1 STEP-THROUGH - $649 $519.

It has been revealed that based in Brooklyn’s Greenpoint neighborhood, Brooklyn Bike Co. uses firsthand knowledge to design well-priced bikes that can withstand the rigors of NYC commutes—and the brand’s Roebling model is a great example. While the Roebling’s design is simple and understated, it’s entirely practical for commuting, fitness, and leisurely rides.

Brooklyn builds the Roebling around a double-butted cromoly frame. Although its skinny tubes look retro compared to the shaped, formed ones used on alloy-framed hybrids, the bike is lightweight (approximately 30 pounds), durable, and easy to ride. The Roebling features a 1x9-speed drivetrain with an 11-41-tooth cassette and 42T chainring. This gives you an easy gear for hills and a significant enough gear for speed on flatter parts of your ride. Unlike many similarly priced hybrids, the Roebling uses V-style rim brakes. While not as flashy as disc brakes, V-brakes are lighterweight and easier to adjust.

If you’re 5’6” or shorter, also check out the Lorimer. It’s essentially the same bike as the Roebling, but in smaller sizes (and in two color options).

Want the easiest-to-maintain, rust-proof hybrid for commuting and riding around town? Then, Priority’s Eight hybrid is probably the best choice you can find. Weighing only 27 pounds, the Eight is lighter than many hybrids thanks to its aluminum frame and carbon fiber fork.

Priority originally introduced its iconic Eight commuter bike in 2016 but discontinued it after a few years. However, the Newly introduced York City-based brand relaunched the model due to rider demand—and it’s a winner. The Eight features a Gates Carbon belt drive drivetrain instead of a standard chain; this system requires no lube or maintenance (other than an occasional wipe-down with a rag). For gearing to scale hills and overpasses, Priority equips the Eight with an eight-speed (hence its name) Shimano Alfine internally geared rear hub with a 307% gear range.

According to recent reports, the Eight comes in traditional and step-through style frames. For all-weather commuters, Priority also offers the Continuum Onyx. It has fenders and dynamo lights that never need charging. Plus, it uses the Enviolo CVT (continuously variable transmission) rear hub. It has the same gear range as a traditional 21-speed drivetrain.

In a recent development, test team member Tom Messina often rides the Cannondale Quick 2 for his daily commutes and on the local rail trail. He’s ridden it through snow squalls and on beautiful fall afternoons, and he’s impressed with the bike’s performance, versatility, and overall value.

“At $949, you’ll be pressed to find many better options on a commuter or introduction bike than this one, especially from a brand I trust as much as Cannondale,” he mentioned. Messina particularly likes the bike’s low weight, wide-range Shimano Cues 9-speed drivetrain, and sure-stopping hydraulic disc brakes. “It’s a top-tier bike for those getting back into riding after a long time off, or spinning the bike path on a sunny day.”.

Want a suspension fork? Cannondale also offers the Quick CX 2 for $1,099.

In a recent development, most hybrids use a road-style frame with a mix of mountain bike and pavement components. Scott takes a slightly different approach with its Scale Gravel series; the result is a blend of mountain bike and gravel tech ideal for adventure riding, backpacking, and commutes in foul weather or worn-out roads.

Intended “to go the distance over any and all types of terrain,” this adventure-ready variant of Scott’s Scale XC racing hardtail features an aluminum frame and carbon fork with multiple attachment points for carrying gear. The Gravel 20 has a SRAM Eagle 70 1x12 drivetrain that provides extremely low gearing, and Shimano hydraulic disc brakes ensure strong stopping power.

Recent findings suggest that while the Gravel 20 is probably way too much bike for most people’s rides, it’s a perfect option if your gravel roads and rides are more extreme than most. However, if you like the look of this bike and want a lighterweight option, Scott offers a range of Scale Gravel models—some with carbon frames and electronic shifting—from $1,700 to $5,500.

This FX 2 earns high marks for its value. Its aluminum frame and fork have a look and feel of some of Trek’s more premium hybrids, without the added price. Internal cable routing keeps the frame looking clean, and like its electrified counterpart, it comes equipped with a Shimano Cues 1x9 drivetrain and Tektro hydraulic disc brakes. At just 26 pounds, it’s impressively light for a bike this capable. Keep the FX 2 as-is for a sleek, fast look, or use the rack and fender mounts for added utility.

Sources indicate that if you want substantial tires for soaking up rough terrain, this isn’t the bike for you. The FX 2 rolls on 35mm tires with a max clearance of 40mm, making it better suited for smooth roads and cinder trails. But if you like a fast, efficient ride, this is a great bike at a great price.

Even though hybrids typically blend road and mountain bike technology and features, many hybrids are biased towards riding pavement and gravel roads rather than trails. However, Polygon’s Heist 2 leans more heavily on its mountain bike DNA.

The Heist’s frame styling closely resembles hardtail mountain bikes, and its geometry isn’t too far from XC racing hardtails from only a decade ago. With a 63mm travel SR Suntour NEX fork and 1x8 Shimano Alivio/Essa drivetrain, you can take the Heist on light-duty singletrack. (Though you might want tires knobbier than the stock WTB Riddlers if you have anything but smooth trails.).

Industry observers note that specialized has sold its Sirrus platform for decades, and that experience reveals in this bike’s details. This bike embodies the “I need it to do everything” ethos.

The Sirrus features sporty geometry for a fast ride feel and a rigid fork to save some weight. Specialized equips the Sirrus X 2.0 with a wide-range Shimano Cues 9-speed drivetrain, hydraulic disc brakes, and 40mm semi-slick tires for some off-pavement use. The Sirrus frame also has mounts for racks (for commuting or touring) and fenders.

BUY SIRRUS X 2.0 STEP-THROUGH - $850.

Many “women’s hybrids” use step-through frames, or are men’s bikes in a different color. As one of cycling’s only brands focused exclusively on women riders, Liv designs its frame geometries and touchpoints (such as saddles and grips) to better fit women’s bodies.

Alight is Liv’s hybrid platform; Alight models feature flat handlebars, rigid forks, 700x38c tires, and an upright riding position. This makes the Alight comfortable and stable without compromising too much speed. You can use the Alight for fitness rides and commutes since Liv equips the bike with mounts for a rack and fenders.

The Alight Disc 2 features a 1x9 MicroShift drivetrain, with an 11-46 tooth cassette and 40T chainring. This gives the Alight a low gear for climbing hills; however, some riders may find the gearing isn’t hard enough for flat sections of road.

It has been revealed that most hybrid models are traditional human-powered bicycles. However, some brands offer hybrid-style electric bikes. These hybrids feature lightweight electric motors and rechargeable batteries to provide pedal assistance up to 20 or 28 mph, depending on local regulations.

In a recent development, below are two electric-assist hybrid bikes we’ve tested and recommend. For more e-bike options, check out our in-depth Electric Bike Buyer’s Guide.

This relatively affordable seven-speed model from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat—and now even more so with hydraulic disc brakes on this revamped version. Push the throttle, and the Soltera’s brushless hub motor kicks in, assisting you more gently as you begin pedaling.

The Soltera features disc brakes, an integrated light, and turn signals. The battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (a surprising feature compared to the bolt-on vibe of many bikes in this price range), which helps the bike blend in with non-electric bikes. Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a 46-pound package.

Many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds, so a sub-40-pound e-bike is rather impressive. Unfortunately, e-bikes this light are usually rather expensive. However, Velotric’s Tempo only costs $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight. Velotric achieves this weight reduction and low cost by ditching the bulky suspension fork and using a smaller battery.

Like most hybrids, and unlike many e-bikes, the Tempo features 700c gravel tires. These tires roll quicker than 26- or 27.5-inch tires on pavement while giving the Tempo improved traction on dirt roads and gravel paths. Velotric offers the Tempo in a traditional double diamond frame and a mid-step design. Both frames are available in two colors and two sizes.

Since riders use hybrids in different ways, brands make various styles of these bikes to meet their needs and budgets. Some focus on lightweight and speed, while others are more rugged and can even tackle some easier mountain bike trails. There are also hybrids with features such as racks, fenders, and lights for commuting and touring, as well as some e-bike models.

Industry observers note that when shopping for a hybrid, I recommend first thinking about where you will ride it most often. If you will mostly ride on paved roads and bike paths, consider a hybrid that focuses on low weight and has slick tires. If you’re commuting, look for bikes with mounts for racks or fenders, and have heavy-duty tires and wheels. For gravel paths or light-duty trail riding, consider hybrid models with suspension forks and knobbier tires.

It has been revealed that lastly, I always remind hybrid shoppers to consider a bike’s long-term use. Look for hybrids that use common, universal-sized components and avoid those with proprietary features or gimmicks. Riders often own their hybrids for several years, sometimes decades. You’ll want to be able to service and repair the bike down the line, especially if you use it for commuting.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

10-Minute Morning Yoga Routine to Wake Up Your Entire Body

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This quick yoga flow at home is, as the name promises, a continuously moving, flowy vinyasa practice for full-body flexibility that moves your body in all the ways you need.
  • According to recent reports, so if you woke up feeling a little sore or stiff, taking yourself through these movements can bring relief and get you feeling more comfortable in your body.
  • No props are required although you are always welcome to use them anytime you would like more support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This quick yoga flow at home is, as the name promises, a continuously moving, flowy vinyasa practice for full-body flexibility that moves your body in all the ways you need. Rather than holding poses for an extended period of time, you’re moving with your breath in a fluid and rhythmic 10-minute yoga routine that will definitely energize you and target your back, hips, and hamstrings.

According to recent reports, so if you woke up feeling a little sore or stiff, taking yourself through these movements can bring relief and get you feeling more comfortable in your body. I encourage you to choose a one-word intention for your day that you pause and focus on at the outset and throughout your practice. What is one word that captures how you want to feel today, what you want to focus on, or what matters to you right now?

No props are required although you are always welcome to use them anytime you would like more support.

Recent findings suggest that you’re going to start by targeting the spine. From your hands and knees, your palms go underneath your shoulders, knees underneath your hips. As you inhale, lower your belly, lift your gaze and arch your back in Cow Pose.

As you exhale, reverse that motion. Thinking of pushing into your fingertips and knuckles, pushing the mat away from you, and letting your head release and your neck relax in Cat Pose.

And then go in between these two poses, getting into all parts of the spine, including the neck, upper back, mid back, lower back, all the way to your tailbone, trying to get that full range of motion.

Come back to hands and knees with a neutral spine.

Still on your hands and knees, lift your right leg and trace some circles with it, as significant as you can, and then let’s reverse the direction of those circles. You’re simply trying to create movement through your right hip. You don’t need to overthink this one.

Recent findings suggest that step your right foot straight out to the side and press the outer edge of your foot against the floor. Lift yourself upright and reach your left arm overhead and toward the right in a side body stretch known as Gate Pose.

Sources indicate that come back to your hands and knees, tuck your toes, and hover your knees a little above the mat. You can probably feel your core engage.

Walk your feet back to keep your shoulders over your wrists in Plank Pose. Strongly press the mat away from you, drawing your lower belly inward and broadening through your upper back. Think of lengthening your tailbone toward your heels and drawing your lower belly inward and upward.

Industry observers note that let’s find Downward-Facing Dog. Lift your hips up and back, and peddle out your feet by straightening one leg and bending the other to stretch your ankles and calves. Keep your arms straight without locking your elbows. Feel the length through your spine.

Lower your knees to the mat and repeat the poses on your left side, including Hip Circles, Gate Pose, Hovering Tabletop, Plank, and Downward-Facing Dog.

From Downward-Facing Dog, reach your right leg toward the sky, bend your right knee, open your hip, and take one more of those major hip circles from your Three-Legged Dog.

From Down Dog, inhale as you step your right foot forward, spin your back foot almost parallel to the short side of the mat as if you were coming into Warrior 2. Exhale as you flow into Extended Side Angle, bringing your right forearm onto your right thigh and reaching your left arm overhead.

As you inhale, straighten your front leg and reach your right arm all the way back in Reverse Triangle.

Then exhale back into Extended Side Angle, sinking your hips a little lower. Repeat that flow twice more like this.

Recent findings suggest that bring both palms to the mat on either side of your right foot and find Pigeon Pose from here. So take your right knee behind your right wrist and reach your left leg straight back. Inhale as you come high onto your fingertips to lift and lengthen, then exhale as you bend forward.

It has been revealed that move in between the two shapes twice more as you undulate through the spine. Then the next time you lower yourself close to the mat, stay here for 5 long, slow breaths. Try to release tension through your shoulder blades and arms.

When you’re ready, lift yourself off the mat and find your Downward-Facing Dog. If you like, you can first come forward into Plank and then lower yourself to the mat and take Cobra. Then repeat these poses on your left side, starting with Three-Legged Dog, Dynamic Extended Side Angle, and Dynamic Pigeon.

Come back to Downward-Facing Dog. Pause here for several breaths.

According to recent reports, bring your knees to the mat and take a seat. As with most morning practices, I don’t include a Savasana in case you might be tempted to fall back asleep, but you’re always welcome to take it on your own.

Sit tall and roll your shoulders down and away from your ears. Maybe you bring your hands together at the front of your heart. Pause here for as long as you can.

Thank you so much for doing this quick vinyasa flow at home with me. May you feel really good and have gotten a boost of energy. Let me know what your intention is for the day ahead in a comment below.

#9889. Breaking: The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

📅 28 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3107 w)

Breaking: The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

📅 28 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”.
  • The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change.
  • Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”.

The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change. Often, the righting reflex is particularly strong in people who really, really care.

Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?

We are now entering upside-down-land.

Motivational Interviewing describes how this (beautiful, well-intentioned) instinct to help can actually hinder a client’s progress.

That’s because when we swoop in to fix, correct, or steer, clients often do the exact opposite of what we’re hoping for: They dig in and get defensive.

Push someone the “right” way and, paradoxically, they’ll start advocating for the very habits they came to you to change. You end up being the one arguing for change—which leaves them to argue against it. Everyone walks away a little more frustrated, and the client feels more stuck than ever.

Sources indicate that instead, great, experienced coaches learn to get curious instead of corrective. (They might even encourage the client to explore not changing!).

That’s just one example of an upside-down skill that separates a good coach from a masterful one. But it’s certainly not the only example.

We asked some of Precision Nutrition’s most seasoned PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certified coaches a simple question:.

What’s something you were sure about early in your career that you later had to unlearn?

Their (honest, and sometimes humbling) answers are below, plus the wiser way forward they adopted, and are now sharing with you.

Our first lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach Jeremy Fernandes, PN2-MHC.

Recent findings suggest that with over 14 years of coaching experience, Coach Jeremy is known for his friendly, comfortable, “talk to me like I’m your buddy” coaching style. Which is ironic, because as you’ll see, he started off his career leaning heavily on a rigid structure that was actually pushing clients away.

Here’s what Coach Jeremy has to say:.

It has been revealed that at the beginning of my career, when I’d been a personal trainer for a year or two, I had a friend ask if I offered nutrition coaching. And my first move was: Here are all of the forms. And when I say “all of the forms,” I mean all of them—I probably sent this person 20 pages to fill out.

Three weeks later I had to hunt them down, and we ended up filling them out together—which took two and a half grueling hours.

If not for those forms, we could have started actually coaching, like, 20 days earlier.

Not long after, another friend highlighted up at my door with this white-hot intensity: “Tell me what to do, I’m ready,” they said. And I immediately dumped a metaphorical bucket of ice water on them with those darn forms. It was radio silence after that.

The problem was that I was operating like my sole job was to extract information from a person and then solve the mystery—as if I had some advanced pattern recognition about you that you didn’t have about yourself.

And unfortunately, I kept on that terrible path for a while.

What finally prompted a change was going through the Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

Going through that course, I saw there was a better framework—one that doesn’t rely on me robotically extracting information.

In a recent development, I learned to let the client take the lead, and then just listen and maybe ask a few good questions. And it works so much better—for everyone.

Industry observers note that now I work from the assumption that my client knows themselves better than anyone. One of my most valuable questions is simply:.

“What have you tried before, what did you like about it, and what didn’t you like?”.

When I let people take the floor, they nail the really significant stuff more often than not—in a way my paperwork and my detective work never facilitated.

It has been revealed that honestly, the forms were me projecting professionalism, because back then I didn’t feel like a professional. My identity as a coach never felt natural until after L2. Now, just letting someone talk feels like coaching. We start with a connection, and then I just let them fill in the gaps.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN Director of Community Engagement and in-house coach Kate Solovieva, PN2-MHC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Kate is known for her honesty and incisiveness. She has a way of dropping realness on her clients that may first feel like a shock, but ultimately ends up getting her clients to the heart of the matter much faster. But one hard truth she had to face was her own.

Here’s what Coach Kate has to say:.

You know the story: You reach the healthy weight, the habits lock in, and the weight just stays stable on its own. You hit “save” and move on with your happily ever after.

And that is not the case at all.

At least most of the time. It’s true, some goals really are like that. If you want to run a marathon, you can pick a race date, follow a training program, show up to the start line, run it—and then you never have to run again and you will still have achieved that goal. That’s a real destination; you cross the finish line once and check the goal off.

But weight loss, muscle gain, body recomposition, building a habit of movement or eating well—those aren’t like that. Especially when the goal means working against a chronic tendency, like a predisposition to high blood pressure, or to hating exercise, or to living in a larger body than you’d prefer.

Industry observers note that those goals come with a pretty good amount of ongoing and intentional maintenance—daily, weekly, monthly. There’s no save button.

In a recent development, this realization didn’t come from one single client or one moment for me. It came through a collection of observations, including observations of myself. But once I saw it, it changed how I coach.

According to recent reports, I realized that if there’s no real finish line, then my job is to manufacture finish lines along the way. That way, my clients continually feel like they’re accomplishing something satisfying.

I take the big goal and break it into something specific and daily—and then I insert smaller outcome goals into the journey.

Sources indicate that for instance, someone going from sedentary to wanting to lose 100 pounds is facing a huge goal, full of behaviors and identities they’ll have to grow into. So along the way, we might set a goal of running a single mile without stopping. Strictly speaking, that doesn’t have much to do with the bigger goal—but it also has everything to do with it. It’s checkable. Achievable. Ideally it’s also something they’re a little excited about: fun, interesting, maybe even a little scary, but still within reach.

Because here’s the thing: It’s very hard to motivate the human brain to work out three times a week for the rest of their life to “get healthier.” “Being healthy” isn’t tangible, it’s not immediate—you can’t feel that far-off outcome in your body.

Recent findings suggest that but striving towards a fun, achievable goal in the next three to six months? That’s real. It also builds in structure, and provides those little spikes of motivation—the hit of dopamine you get from working hard at something and actually accomplishing it.

Recent findings suggest that health isn’t something we ever fully “accomplish” or check off. So we have to give ourselves these little concrete goals along the way that we can feel and see and be delighted by.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN content creator Azul Corajoria, CPT, PN2-MHC.

With over nine years of coaching experience, Coach Azul’s coaching fingerprint is empathetic, relatable, and endlessly encouraging.

While these traits always came naturally to her, for a long time, she thought she had to adopt an opposite style to help certain clients (and herself) to “get back in line” when habits didn’t go as planned.

Here’s what Coach Azul has to say:.

Early in my coaching career, I thought that if someone wasn’t following through on what they said they would do, it’s because they needed more structure or just to get their “head in the game.”.

I couldn’t understand why someone would invest in coaching and then not do the things we planned.

It was especially confusing because most of my clients had “discipline.” They were successful, responsible, hardworking people who showed up for their jobs, families, and everyone else in their lives.

Meanwhile, I was also “disciplined” in many areas of my life—yet I also struggled with eating well and exercising consistently.

According to recent reports, at this time, I felt this lack of consistency was my fault, and went straight to being really angry at myself. I thought I was just missing the “perfect something” (the perfect workout, the perfect diet) to help me change, so I’d just move from thing to thing, but each one would bring fresh disappointment.

I was incredibly frustrated by this cycle, and my response was to get stricter and harsher with myself.

It has been revealed that it’s hard to say when it all changed. It wasn’t an overnight epiphany; it was a culmination of years of getting curious, being open to different methods, like the Body Positivity Movement and Intuitive Eating. I dove into self-compassion and positive psychology research, and I went through the PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

According to recent reports, I applied everything I learned, and I noticed that the more open and curious I was, the better my clients responded. Slowly, that turned into the realization that the more open and curious I was with myself, the better I would respond.

Sources indicate that I stopped binge eating. I started enjoying exercise more. I took more career risks.

I learned that when we can respond to a setback with curiosity instead of punishment, we’re much more likely to stay engaged. When I allow myself to be disappointed by an action, take responsibility for it, and remain on my own side, I feel safer reflecting and taking risks. The more I do that, the more likely I am to achieve the things I want.

Sometimes the most helpful thing we can teach a client (and ourselves) is not how to push harder or “just be more disciplined.” It’s how to make a mistake, remain on our own side, and keep going.

Industry observers note that because self-compassion is not the opposite of accountability; it’s often what makes accountability possible. (I call it “compassionate accountability.”).

None of us will ever be the “perfect” coach, and we don’t have to be. The more human I’ve allowed myself to be, the better relationships I’ve had with my clients. My biggest goal as a coach is to create an environment my client feels safe to come back to with not only their wins, but their losses. The safer they feel being honest and open with me, the safer they’ll feel to try upcoming things—and over time they’ll build the confidence to do it themselves.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Dom Matteo, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

Recent findings suggest that with over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Dom stands out for his non-judgemental attitude and excellent listening skills. For Dom, these traits are relatively inherent, but they’ve also been carefully developed and honed, in part by letting go of what he calls the “coach’s ego”—the assumption that he already knew what a client’s success should look like, and that he was the one who got to keep score.

Here’s what Coach Dom has to say:.

I took that stated goal at face value, and treated whatever number they gave me as the measuring stick, as the most vital thing to work towards.

But then, I’d see a client struggling to do their actions even 50 percent of the time, and I’d think: ‘This person is never going to be happy, because this won’t get them to the goal weight they told me they wanted.’.

Remember, I assumed the number was the real goal.

However, again and again, those same clients would turn out to be genuinely happy with their progress, not because they hit their exact goal, but because they felt so much better about themselves and their lives.

It has been revealed that what I learned is that the stated outcome was almost never the true goal for many of them. When they stated ‘lose 50 pounds,’ what they really meant was: I want to feel better. And being consistent even half the time, over a year, netted results they were thrilled with. Because they felt better. They felt different.

It has been revealed that so the thing I had to let go of was my own scorecard. Who am I to tell a client that what they’re doing isn’t good enough, if they’re happy with how things are going?

My new definition of progress became less about approaching a specific final number and more about another question: “Am I a little better today than I was yesterday?”.

These days, I spend time up front helping a client build what we call a “wellness vision.” We clarify their values, and what success actually looks and feels like to them.

According to recent reports, then, instead of assuming I know how to measure their progress, I’ll ask: “How will you know if this is helping? How do you want to measure success?”.

According to recent reports, the result is that even a client who’s fixated on the scale can see other signs of progress long before the scale actually changes. And often, those other signs are the things they really wanted to change in the first place.

According to recent reports, it turns out the most useful thing I can provide isn’t a judgement about whether a client is succeeding. Instead, it’s to help them determine and notice their own success, by their own measures.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Jason Bonn, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 18 years of coaching experience, Coach Jason’s clients describe him as patient, observant, and deeply dedicated. He has a knack for spotting a client’s potential—though as you’ll read in this story, Coach Jason learned that getting too focused on a specific version of that potential sometimes kept him from seeing other ways his clients could grow and thrive.

Here’s what Coach Jason has to say:.

For me, progress felt like a puzzle to solve: I’d play with adjustments to exercise volume or intensity, calorie or protein intake, eating more slowly, eating to 80 percent fullness, all the fundamental stuff.

But then, because of one client I still think about, I began to shift how I thought about “progress.”.

According to recent reports, he was in our PN coaching program. He lost 40 to 50 pounds in his first six months—which was great—but then everything stalled.

We tried adjustment after adjustment for the next two and a half years. We added more protein, more cardio, and worked through his particular peccadillo, eating corn chips at night. But none of it moved his numbers.

What got me was that he kept showing up anyway: three straight years, re-enrolling each time, even though the scale had plateaued.

That told me something was working for him—it just wasn’t something I recognized yet.

Recent findings suggest that in his third year, we stopped looking only at the gym and his diet, and started looking at his whole life. He was a landscape painter, so we built his practices around that instead: make a sketch or work on a painting daily, anything that sparked some joy or interest. Within a couple of weeks, he was getting on his bike and riding out to further places for different scenery to paint.

In part because of this client, I’m now a lot more cognizant of coaching the whole person, and considering their Deep Health. Weight and performance numbers are just one piece of a much bigger picture that includes relationships, emotional wellbeing, and what someone finds meaningful.

I’ve also stopped zeroing in on “problem” behavior.

I try to understand a person’s life overall—not just the behavior I’ve been hired to help with—because there’s a connectedness to it all, and behavior tends to emerge within the context of someone’s life.

I’ve also stopped treating the coaching relationship as a means to an outcome and started treating it as the main thing—the sun that everything orbits, the glue that holds it all together.

That client kept coming back for three years because the relationship mattered to him. By the end, I’d stopped thinking I was failing him. The weight loss was such a small part of the success. The relationship was the bigger piece.

It has been revealed that coaching mastery isn’t about stockpiling more information. (Your clients can Google information or ask a chatbot, and so can you.).

It’s about developing the judgment to know when to use what you know, when to set it aside, and when the most helpful thing you can do is nothing at all, except be there.

But that kind of judgment is hard to build alone; it takes practice, expert feedback, and a few humbling moments with real clients—which is exactly what the PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certification is designed to offer.

With enough practice, self-awareness, and the right training, you can gain the wisdom and skill of the above coaches.

But the best coaches, it turns out, are defined less by what they know than by what they’ve been willing to unlearn.

Ready to move from competent to truly masterful—in 20 weeks?

The PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification is an advanced, practice-based program designed for coaches who want to work at a deeper level—and do it sooner than the traditional 5–10 year path.

This is not a nutrition course.

It’s a mentored, small-group experience that prepares you to:.

You’ll learn directly from PN’s most experienced coaches through weekly live mentorship, structured self-study, and real-world coaching practice.

Level 2 is NBHWC-approved, making graduates eligible for:.

These credentials expand your career options and set you apart in an increasingly crowded field.

💡 Key Takeaways
