  • Turn your swim workouts into games with these fun ideas for making the pool more enjoyable.
  • Industry observers note that we know all the excuses to skip a swim because we’ve used many of them ourselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Turn your swim workouts into games with these fun ideas for making the pool more enjoyable. (Photo: Challenge Family).

Industry observers note that we know all the excuses to skip a swim because we’ve used many of them ourselves. Either it’s too cold outside or it’s too beautiful a day to pass up a bike ride. Or perhaps there’s a storm 100 miles away that might suddenly decide to blow right over the aquatics center. But the truth is, if your workout is interesting enough, you’ll have all the excuses you need to get yourself into the pool, not out of it.

According to recent reports, and we’re not just talking about adding in a random drill here and there. Gamifying your swim workout, whether through solo exercises or team activities, helps make a workout enticing enough that you’ll want to do it over and over again. Adding an element of play to your swim can make it more challenging, productive, and fun all at once.

Before we get into a handful of our favorite games and drills, we asked Sage Hopkins, head coach of Women’s Swimming & Diving at San José State University, for his tips on how to make swimming more enjoyable. With these tools in your arsenal, you might not skip your pool workouts anymore, but actually look forward to them instead.

In a recent development, first, Hopkins stresses how crucial it is to hear laughter echoing across the pool deck. This might not be possible if you’re training alone, but if you have a training buddy who always keeps you smiling, make it a priority to meet with them more regularly. Hopkins also encourages using music to establish an upbeat atmosphere; that might look like playing a pump-up song on your way to the pool, or investing in a pair of swimming headphones to keep the tunes going lap after lap.

Recent findings suggest that once you know your purpose, Hopkins states, it’s easier to figure out what kinds of activities will make swimming more meaningful and enjoyable. Those who enjoy the camaraderie aspect of swimming and triathlon will enjoy team games like sharks and minnows.

In a recent development, even simple details like naming a set, Hopkins indicates, can add a thrill to swimming. If there’s a test set you’re always dreading, give it a quirky or amusing name to make it seem less intimidating. You could use the most challenging triathlon you’ve ever lined up for as inspiration (The Wales One Hundreds, for instance, or the Norseman No Breathers).

Now, without further ado, let the games begin!

You don’t need any fancy clubs to play a round of swim golf — just enough glycogen in your head to add numbers. Hopkins suggests this drill for data-driven triathletes because it’s easy to keep track of your progression over time. Essentially, you add the number of strokes with the number of seconds that it takes you to complete a certain distance (such as 50 yards) to get a “score.” You’ll then repeat that distance several times within a single set, trying to keep your score as low as possible. This game helps improve your distance per stroke and ultimately conserve energy.

Healthy suspense invites bursts of dopamine and curiosity into your workout, and it also means that there’s no one to blame but fate for back-to-back sprint sets. Make sure to write the following rules down on a whiteboard or protected piece of paper to reduce confusion.

It has been revealed that start by grabbing a set of waterproof playing cards, and assign a technique to each suit; for example, spades might call for kicking, hearts for drills, diamonds for swimming, and clubs for pulling. Next, assign a distance to groups of numbers (for instance, 2s and 3s might mean 50s, while 4s and 5s might mean 100s, and so on). Keep your jacks, queens, kings, and aces in a separate pile because they’ll dictate the number of repeats (1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively).

Industry observers note that so, for example, pulling a 5 of clubs alongside a queen would require you to grab your pull buoy for 2×100. Pulling a 2 of hearts alongside an ace would mean a 5×50 drill.

In a recent development, another way to bring a measure of unpredictability to your workout is to roll a single die four times to determine your next set. The first roll determines your technique (5s could require kicking), the second your effort level (perhaps 4s always mean sprints), the third your distance (1s could mean 50s), and the fourth your number of reps (anywhere from 1 to 6).

It has been revealed that if you were on a summer swim team as a kid, chances are high you played many games of sharks and minnows. The game starts out with one “shark” who tries to tag all the other “minnows” as they swim from one side of the pool to the other. Each swimmer who gets tagged turns into a shark for the next round. You can complicate this game by instituting an underwater safety zone.

It has been revealed that if you have an area of the pool to yourself, form teams, set up goals on opposite walls with pull buoys, grab a ball, and play water polo. This is an excellent way to make vertical kicking, sprinting, and treading water more exciting. It also facilitates team bonding.

Head to the deep end for this game to work on endurance as you tread water and practice vertical kicking. If the lifeguards allow it, you can play water volleyball over the flags with an inflatable beach ball. Your pool might even have a water volleyball net, and some versions float so that you can move them as required.

Hopkins recommends “call it sets,” inspired by Bob Steele, to work on pacing and fine-tuning your internal clock. Essentially, you and your training partners will swim a set of 100s, and before each repeat, each one of you will predict the time you expect to hit. Whoever is closest to their estimates wins the set.

Sources indicate that chase sets are a fun way for training groups with seemingly disparate ability levels to unite, indicates Hopkins. Slower swimmers are allowed a head start, while faster swimmers are tasked with trying to catch them. Chase sets are ideally employed for speedwork, not drills.

Casino night is extraordinarily fun for large teams and helps highlight everyone’s unique talents. First, two or three swimmers who are roughly equivalent in speed line up at the blocks. Then, the other teammates line up behind the swimmer they predict will win.

Industry observers note that from there, you’ll use cards or dice to determine the “event” that the swimmers will be competing in (see general rules above in the solo workouts). Whoever has picked the winning swimmer gets a rest break while the rest of the team completes a penalty swim (a 50 sprint, perhaps). If you have one seemingly unbeatable swimmer on the team, you can assign them a permanent handicap.

Breaking: 5 Cross-Training Workouts for Seniors

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2436 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve never prioritized strength training as part of your fitness routine, it’s not too late to start.
  • A recent study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism recruited two groups of senior participants.
  • This doesn’t mean you should wait for your golden years to pick up a dumbbell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve never prioritized strength training as part of your fitness routine, it’s not too late to start.

A recent study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism recruited two groups of senior participants. Individuals in the first group were between 65 and 75 years old, and those in the second group were 85 years and older. Neither group had engaged in resistance training for at least six months. After following a 12-week strength-training program, both cohorts highlighted significant improvements in muscle mass, strength, and physical performance.

This doesn’t mean you should wait for your golden years to pick up a dumbbell. Age-related sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and function, can begin in your 30s, says Robert Linkul, C.S.C.S., owner of Training The Older Adult. And it only ramps up with every passing decade. “There’s a constant battle against sarcopenia,” he tells Bicycling. “But if you resistance train your entire life, your body shouldn’t change drastically. Naturally, you’ll lose some muscle mass. There’s going to be some degeneration of performance and power output. But as long as you keep trying to maintain it, you’ll have it.”.

Julie Logue, M.P.H., senior program manager for Silver Sneakers, agrees that strength training is particularly worthwhile for seniors. “As muscular strength and endurance improves, you can perform activities of daily living with greater ease,” she says, noting that a regular resistance training program can also help older individuals maintain bone density, improve balance, reduce the risk of falling, and correct muscle imbalances. “Because cycling uses some parts of the body more than others, strength training is a necessary complement to promote muscle balance and reduce overuse injuries. Increasing strength can also benefit cyclists by increasing overall endurance and postural control,” she says.

Convinced but not sure where to start? With Linkul’s help, we put together five strength-training workouts you can do on cross-training days. Each one includes senior-appropriate exercises, some of which can be modified or progressed depending on your skill level and experience. For exercises that require added resistance, choose a load that’s heavy but doable; on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being your max effort, aim for between a 6 and 7.

Cyclists who are entirely latest to strength training want to go lighter at first. “Beginning with bodyweight movements can help build a foundation for using external resistance,” Logue states. She also recommends consulting a primary care provider before starting any new exercise program.

According to recent reports, like most bodyweight workouts, you can do this full-body circuit anywhere, making it a convenient option for when you’re traveling, can’t get to the gym, or just don’t feel like dealing with a bunch of equipment. You’ll work every major muscle group, including your deep core, and train functional, everyday movement patterns, like standing from a sitting position, pushing up from the floor, and maintaining balance and control while stepping backward.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a chair, box, or bench.

Stand in front of a chair, box, or bench with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Tap the chair with glutes. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and body forming straight line from head to feet. Drive right foot to chest. Step back to plank. Repeat on left side. Continue alternating. Do 15 reps per side.

Industry observers note that stand with feet hip-width apart. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward. Repeat, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

According to recent reports, start faceup with arms at sides, legs together, and feet on an elevated surface, like a small box, bench, or chair. Engage core and lift hips off ground so body forms a straight line from heels to shoulders. (Head and shoulders stay on ground, like a straight-leg glute bridge.) Allow arms to rest on ground or, for added difficulty, lift them off floor so elbows are straight and fingertips point up. Hold for 30-60 seconds.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Recent findings suggest that start in plank position, shoulders over wrists and forming straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows, lowering body to floor while maintaining straight line. Press back up to plank. Repeat. Do 12 reps. Perform on knees or with hands against wall to make it easier.

This workout develops core strength through exercises that challenge your balance and train transferable skills, like carrying a heavy load, crawling in multiple directions, and shifting your body weight from a lying-down position. The single-leg glute bridge and superman variation fire up the posterior chain, which is critical for cyclists, and the three-way toe tap will help improve your overall balance and stability.

In a recent development, perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a dumbbell or kettlebell.

Sources indicate that start on hands and knees, shoulders over wrists and knees under hips. Lift knees just about an inch off floor. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the right. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot backward. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the left. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot forward. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps.

Stand with feet together. Send hips back, back flat and core engage, to lower into a shallow hinge position. Keeping weight on left leg, tap right foot forward, then back to left foot. Tap right foot out to the side, then back to left foot. Tap right foot backward, then back to left foot. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Tap right hand to left shoulder. Then return to plank. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Holding a dumbbell or kettlebell in one hand, stand tall with shoulders back, chin parallel to the floor, and arms straight down at sides. Keep shoulders over hips (be careful not to lean away from weighted arm) and relax shoulders as you slowly walk forward for 30-60 seconds. Repeat, holding weight on opposite side.

Lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted, arms down by sides. Lift and straighten right leg, knees in line. Drive through left foot to lift hips up. Pause, then slowly lower back down. Lift with glutes and hamstrings, rather than low back. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Industry observers note that A dedicated upper-body workout counteracts the time cyclists spend leaning forward in a rounded position and can help correct postural problems, alleviate back pain, and lead to better performance on the bike. This workout includes both pushing and pulling movement patterns and targets the muscles of the chest, back, shoulders, arms, and core.

It has been revealed that perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, and a medicine ball.

It has been revealed that start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg bent or straight (whatever is more comfortable). Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. #9884. Tech Report: What Yoga Can Teach You About Quieting Your Thoughts

Tech Report: What Yoga Can Teach You About Quieting Your Thoughts

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it’s one thing to practice yoga and to think maybe you’ll try meditation one of these times.
  • In order to embrace meditation, I found it incredibly helpful to study yoga philosophy and try to understand why I’m practicing.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali is generally considered the primary source for yoga philosophy, although some scholars question how this came to be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s one thing to practice yoga and to think maybe you’ll try meditation one of these times. It’s another to understand how these practices can support you in everyday life. In his latest book, accessible yoga teacher and YJ contributor Jivana Heyman explains the connection among yoga, meditation, and how you navigate your days. Although books explaining poses and esoteric theories abound, Heyman’s Yoga Meditation: Finding a Path Back to Your Self explains how these apply to any situation through storytelling, relatable examples, and insightful questions you can contemplate or rely on as journal prompts. The following excerpt helps you understand the connection so you can begin to try it in your own life.—Renee Marie Schettler, Editor in Chief, YJ.

In order to embrace meditation, I found it incredibly helpful to study yoga philosophy and try to understand why I’m practicing. I realize that many people find philosophy boring, but I always recommend that my students begin meditation with some understanding of the philosophical concepts behind the practice.

Recent findings suggest that the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali is generally considered the primary source for yoga philosophy, although some scholars question how this came to be. There is also a debate among scholars about the date of the text, which may be anywhere from 2200 to 1500 years old. Personally, I think the Sutras have staying power because Patanjali consolidated thousands of years of teachings into a relatively terse collection of 196 incredibly insightful aphorisms.

The reason I love starting our meditation conversation with the Sutras is that it offers much insight into how the mind works, as well as how to use yoga to work with the mind. His main goal is to teach us to quiet our mind so that we can experience the eternal true Self, or spirit.

Recent findings suggest that yoga is a process of remembering who we really are and what Patanjali does, in a variety of ways, is show us how to do just that. We don’t need to become something else or earn enlightenment. In fact, my favorite thing about the Sutras is that he starts with the positive assumption that we are spirit and the recognition that our spiritual nature has been obscured by the mind’s attachments and desires. In other words, there’s nothing to gain, just a lot to release.

In the very beginning of the Sutras, Patanjali offers what is considered the definition of yoga: “Yogah chitta vritti nirodhah.” (1.2) which is often translated as, “Yoga is the stilling of the changing states of the mind.” 20 It is a surprising statement because he’s saying that quieting the thoughts and emotions in the mind is both the practice of yoga and the state of yoga—union with the true self.

According to recent reports, so right off the bat, Patanjali is already talking about the practice of meditation and working with the mind. In the next Sutra, he goes on to say that, “When that is accomplished, the Seer abides in its own true nature.” (1.3) 21 In other words, when the mind quiets down and you find stillness, you experience peace, joy, and bliss—whatever words you’d like to use for the experience of your divinity.

It has been revealed that according to Patanjali, the process of quieting the mind begins with concentration, which is at the heart of meditation. He’s open-minded about what we’re concentrating on. Instead, he emphasizes the process of concentration. He explains that you can remove the obstacles to the experience of yoga, “By meditating on anything one chooses that is elevating.” (1.39) 22.

Consciously working to quiet the mind is a theme throughout his treatise on yoga. In other words, the entirety of the text is basically about meditation. He goes on to expound on the contents of the mind, the obstacles to practice, how to avoid suffering, and eventually he describes the eight limbs of yoga, which is essentially a detailed meditation program.

According to recent reports, there’s a reason Patanjali devotes the Sutras to working with the mind. Because of the nature of the mind, as well as our noisy culture, we seem to have a distorted understanding of ourselves. We have identified with our body and mind, yet these are the parts of us that are always changing. Instead, Patanjali is asking us to identify with the part that is eternal—our unchanging spirit.

It’s also interesting to consider how asana (yoga poses) is considered in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali. In this text, asana doesn’t simply lead us to meditation, it is meditation. People often recite Patanjali’s definition of, “Asana is a steady, comfortable posture,” (2.46) 34 but they neglect to include the next sutra, which explains how to practice asana. “By lessening the natural tendency for restlessness and by meditating on the infinite, posture is mastered.” (2.47) 35.

It has been revealed that there are a few major takeaways here: First, the key to asana is meditation. Second, Patanjali admits that the mind is naturally restless. So it might be natural to find meditation challenging: It’s in the mind’s nature to constantly move from one thing to another. He is offering asana as a prescription for a busy mind.

According to recent reports, in the very next sutra, Patanjali describes the result of practicing asana: “Thereafter one is undisturbed by the dualities.” (2.48) 36 He’s revealing the truth of asana as a technique for handling the ups and downs of life. Asana not only prepares the body to take a comfortable seat in meditation, it also lifts us above the chaos of life to find a still point of peace.

So many spiritual, and even meditative, practices are conceptual, intellectual, and ethereal. They can feel too subtle to grasp. But the practice of asana is different. It is practical and grounded in its ability to give you access to deeper parts of yourself, whether you have the patience for seated meditation or not.

In a flowing asana series, you can explore the interplay of action and stillness in your body while your mind focuses on each movement. Or you can hold a static posture and notice dynamic inner movement. You can experience the lifting and grounding that you find in the flow of the breath. The inhale bringing in newly introduced life, the exhalation letting go; inhale lift, exhale release.

It has been revealed that asana allows you to experience the energy of creation moving through the body and mind. By holding steady, or through movement, stretching, or strengthening, asana clears the subtle energetic pathways and allows your prana to flow.

It has been revealed that asana is about expanding your sense of self, yet it’s so often taught in a way that feels limiting or constricting. So many of people struggle with body image, and it’s heartbreaking to think that the way contemporary yoga is taught feeds into this. Instead, yoga can teach you how to cherish your body for giving you this lifetime and for allowing you to engage in spiritual practice. Remember, your body is equally worthy of asana as any other body.

Recent findings suggest that the body has an essential role in the hatha yoga traditions. It’s perceived as either an obstacle that needs to be overcome, or a vehicle that needs to be strong enough to withstand the force of kundalini, potential prana, flowing through it. Some of the more ascetic, or strictly disciplined, traditions focused on overcoming attachment to the body by forcing it into compliance. These hatha yogis would stand for months on end, hold one arm up in the air, or perform some similarly intense practice. This is a way to force the body into compliance in the hope of releasing attachment to it.

It has been revealed that contemporary yoga has maintained a hint of this extreme practice by teaching that the body needs to be whipped into shape in order to be worthy. I don’t think this is a useful idea because it reinforces cultural messages of unworthiness that are used to sell wellness “solutions” back to you. It also feeds the self-hatred and internalized prejudice that flows from ableism, racism, sexism, fat phobia, homophobia, transphobia, ageism, and other kinds of oppression.

You can practice asana as meditation and make movement your practice. You don’t even have to identify as someone who meditates, and you don’t have to sit with your thoughts and feelings. Instead, you can move your body, channel your energy, and find relief from your mind’s ruminations. Your yoga mat or chair is a magic portal to a different land. Take a few breaths, move your body, and then integrate movement with your breath, and poof! Off you go.

In a recent development, because of the way asana is represented in the media as an extreme sport, it can be intimidating for a lot of people, which is why I’ve spent my entire career teaching people how to make these practices accessible and welcoming. The meditative heart of asana practice is naturally inclusive and accessible. Rather than performing asana or copying what other people do, the question is: Can you listen to your own body? When you practice, let go of your thoughts and focus on how you feel, and what your body needs today.

Industry observers note that there are a few different things you can focus on in asana that turns movement into meditation. In fact, you can start by asking yourself what the difference is between asana and exercise. The difference is subtle, and it all comes back to meditation. Is your mind focused when you’re doing asanas? It doesn’t really matter what it’s focused on, but it’s the act of focusing that is key. Mindful awareness is what makes a movement into an asana and into a yoga practice. In the end, you can focus on any of these things:.

Approach a short asana session as a meditation. You can do this with any asana practice focused on your breath. If you have a regular asana practice, do some poses that you enjoy—in a chair or on a yoga mat.

If you are latest to asana, consider joining a beginner’s yoga class, or look up chair yoga online. It can be helpful to start in a chair, or even better, a couch. Couch yoga is my favorite way to experience the power of asana as a meditation.

Effective GLP-1 coaching means understanding these physiological changes and knowing how to adapt your support accordingly.

#9881. What Top Tri Coaches Fix Between November and March

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1647 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

What Top Tri Coaches Fix Between November and March

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season.
  • One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.
  • With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season. (Photo: FinisherPix/Triathlete, Aaron Palaian, Oliver Baker, and courtesy David Tilbury-Davis).

One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.

With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.

According to recent reports, for Northern Hemisphere athletes, that time is now. So, to help you along the way, we turned to four of the sport’s leading coaches to get their views — in their words — on what triathletes should focus on between now and March.

One of the world’s leading coaches and applied sports scientists in endurance sport, Plews has coached elite triathletes, including world champions Chelsea Sodaro, Javier Gomez, and Terenzo Bozzone.

He is also the founder of the coaching platform Endure IQ for both athletes and coaches. Plews himself is a former age-group Ironman world champion and still holds the fastest amateur time at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship.

In a recent development, “I never did proper strength training when I was younger, but now that I do a lot more, I’m seeing the benefits. But it is only as good as the quality and intent you put in. One of the substantial mistakes I see with many triathletes is that there’s no real intent.

“Get someone to help make sure you’re doing proper lifts. If you need to learn the correct movements, winter would be an ideal time. Then strength work needs to challenge the system. We typically talk “reps in reserve” when it comes to strength training [i.e., how many more reps you could complete before reaching failure].

“I’d advise working to two to three reps in reserve, but you can go to four if you’re not confident. But the main thing is you want to see a change in the speed of movement as you fatigue through the set.

It has been revealed that “I would focus mostly on compound lifts: barbell hip thrusts, Bulgarian split squats, Nordic hamstring curls, and isometric holds and calf raises to add injury prevention. As time goes on, pair it with more plyometric and ballistic exercises, which might be a squat into a box jump.”.

“Winter can be a period where you become unstuck from a psychological point of view. What’s vital is to find balance. You want the volume, but don’t want to become stale so that by the time you get to the season, you’ve lost enthusiasm.

According to recent reports, “If you really push the envelope early, especially with long, cold rides in January and February, by the time you get through to the season, you’re just sick of it. So, I think there’s a very fine line between doing too much training and not enough.”.

The founder and head coach of NVDM Coaching in Austin, Texas, Van Der Merwe leads a team of more than 30 coaches supporting over 700 athletes. A former top-50 world-ranked junior tennis player from South Africa, she raced as a professional triathlete from 2010 to 2023 and has coached since 2009. She also leads Ironman U, Ironman’s official coaching certification program.

“Winter is when we raise the ceiling. We reverse periodize, so short, focused threshold and VO2 work comes before the long volume, because every triathlete races at a percentage of their FTP.

“If an athlete raises FTP from 220 to 235 watts this winter and rides an Ironman at 70% of it, race-day power goes from 154 to about 165 watts. Spring then becomes about extending that fitness.”.

“Most athletes book a fit in spring, which leaves little time to adapt before racing. Our order is comfort first, then aerodynamics, then power, because the fastest position is the one you can hold for the whole bike leg and still run well afterward.

“In one study, the lowest torso angle tested cost riders about 16 watts at threshold compared with their own positions. Winter trainer rides are the perfect place to build into a fresh position gradually.”.

Recent findings suggest that “This is one most athletes never think about, and it can quietly derail a whole season. Vitamin D drops through the winter, especially for athletes training indoors at northern latitudes.

“A review of more than 2,000 athletes found over half had inadequate levels. Iron stores matter too, especially for female athletes. We ask athletes to get a baseline panel with vitamin D and ferritin now, so their doctor can address anything before the massive training blocks start.”.

According to recent reports, head coach at KIS Coaching, Cunnama is a former elite professional triathlete from South Africa who won major long-distance races, including Challenge Roth and Ironman Hamburg, and owns two top-five finishes at the Ironman World Championship in Kona. Following his racing career, he became a presenter with the Global Triathlon Network (GTN), sharing his knowledge and experience with a worldwide triathlon audience.

“Everyone knows they should work on their weaknesses over winter, but that usually translates to a broad goal like, ‘I want to work on my swim,’ which then turns into ‘more swimming, less biking and running.’.

It has been revealed that “I find it more effective to keep a balance in all three triathlon disciplines, but try to get ahead on the things that you always fell behind on last season. Determine which aspect of your training made you feel most underconfident, and then tweak your off-season training to target that area.

Sources indicate that “For example, if you found that using paddles destroyed your arms, do extra paddle work. If hills were your nemesis on the bike, hit the hills (or simulate them on the trainer). Rather than tackling physical limitations, target the mental hurdles – use the off-season to get to a place where you love the sessions you hated last season.”.

“It is hard to make changes to technique during the season when you have volume goals in training, because technique changes (or position changes on the bike) require you to only do as much of the new technique as you can sustain, and no more.

It has been revealed that “You can’t ingrain a new technique when the second half of your session is falling back to the old technique! So, make those changes in the off-season and slowly build back that technique better. The advantage of triathlon is you have two other sports to keep you fit while you reset your technique in the third sport.”.

A highly respected triathlon coach, Tilbury-Davis has worked with professional and age-group athletes since 1995. Through Tilbury-Davis Coaching, he has coached leading athletes such as Lionel Sanders and Ashleigh Gentle. Based in Finland, he works with a small group of international athletes.

“Efficiency of movement sounds vague, but while I’m a big proponent of doing strength and conditioning work throughout the year, winter is a time to understand that swimming, biking, and running all require expression of force from the core – when I say core, I effectively mean from the knees to the chest.

“You’re talking around 64 different muscles and creating the capacity to have a stable base to express force from will improve your body alignment in the water, your ability to maintain an aero position on the bike, and your ability to have hip extension and knee drive in the run. It centers around doing the kind of exercises that are multi-plane, multi-muscle recruiting as part of a several-times-a-week program.

In a recent development, “For example, you see a lot of triathletes train with a Masters group and the swim coach says to do a high elbow or chicken wing drill. The reality is that 99% of triathletes do not have sufficient mobility to swim in a manner that a swim coach would like. So, to step back, I would say to improve your swimming, go away and work on your thoracic and scapular mobility.”.

According to recent reports, “A lot of people don’t talk about saddle choice. We all buy expensive running shoes that are made out of expensive foam that breaks down over a period of time, but we forget that saddles are also made out of foam.

“If you’re serious about maintaining a good position on the bike, you probably should be changing your saddle once a year and for a pro that might be twice a year because the foam in the saddle breaks down the same way that the foam in a running shoe breaks down.”.

“Get used to having to cope with uneven surfaces on the run, shortening and lengthening your stride length, stepping over rocks and roots, dealing with off camber, on camber, dealing with gravel, sand, mud, all of those proprioceptive stimuli that vary significantly improve your body’s ability to be efficient. A worst-case scenario for me would be an athlete that just runs on a treadmill the entire winter at a very narrow bandwidth of running paces.

Industry observers note that “A good way of explaining this is that people talk about the way the Kenyans train. They do this famous long run in Iten where it’s a progressively descending pace. But what’s special about that workout is that they’re running on trails, gravel fire roads, wooded areas, and gradient changes. Probably the most powerful thing about that run is that they’re working on different surfaces, different terrains, different obstacles, different gradients, while they’re still working on a physiological stimulus.”.

“That’s probably when people ask me what’s the number-one most crucial session for Ironman training: I would say go run on trails before anything else, because it builds resilience and strength, which is what you need for an Ironman.”.

#9880. Herniated Discs Are a Common Cycling Injury—Here’s Everything You Need to Know

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2302 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Herniated Discs Are a Common Cycling Injury—Here’s Everything You Need to Know

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2302 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sometimes it happens with a bang, like when former Tour de France pro Marty Jemison was racing Tour of Flanders in the late 1990s.
  • Sources indicate that jemison finished the race and the others that followed until he retired about 18 months later, though he had pain off the bike and for the first 30 or 60 minutes of riding, and knew something was wrong.
  • Other times, it’s the proverbial straw that breaks the camel’s (or the cyclist’s) back, as was the case with avid long-distance cyclist Mark Elsasser of Philadelphia who developed some sciatica in 2018.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes it happens with a bang, like when former Tour de France pro Marty Jemison was racing Tour of Flanders in the late 1990s. His saddle slipped to be nose up. He thought “no big deal” until one of the steep cobbled climbs, where he was in the saddle cranking out maximum wattage.“And my back just popped,” he says.

Sources indicate that jemison finished the race and the others that followed until he retired about 18 months later, though he had pain off the bike and for the first 30 or 60 minutes of riding, and knew something was wrong. That something was a herniated disc that became nearly debilitating after retirement, eventually required two procedures, and still flares up to this day if he’s not meticulous about his bike position and on top of his core work.

Other times, it’s the proverbial straw that breaks the camel’s (or the cyclist’s) back, as was the case with avid long-distance cyclist Mark Elsasser of Philadelphia who developed some sciatica in 2018. He was able to ride through it just fine, but couldn’t sit for any length of time before the pain was unbearable. The diagnosis: a herniated disc in his low back, which he resolved with physical therapy and has kept at bay by changing his position on the bike, going from a 0-rise to 5-degree stem. “My spine is less compromised being a bit more upright rather than nose down on top of the stem,” he says.

Herniated discs are fairly common in the general population, occurring most frequently among 30- to 50-year-old adults, and men more often than women. Interestingly, you may have one right now and not even know it. “We know from radiographical studies that 50 percent of those aged 40 may have some form of disc herniation. We might consider it normal, age-related changes, and many of those won’t be symptomatic,” states bike fitter and sports physiotherapist Bianca Broadbent, co-owner of The Cycling Physios based in the United Kingdom.

In fact, one research review published in the American Journal of Neuroradiology found that degenerative changes in the discs, which include herniated discs, are present in nearly 90 percent of adults 60 and older and often require no intervention. A herniated disc only causes pain if it’s pressing or otherwise irritating a nerve root in the spine.

Join Bicycling All Access for more injury-prevention tips and training advice!

It has been revealed that your spine is comprised of 24 vertebrae. Between those vertebrae are fluid-filled cushions known as discs, which act as shock absorbers for your spinal bones.

“Imagine your spinal discs as jelly-filled doughnuts,” says Andrew Pruitt, Ed.D., the founder of the Boulder Center for Sports Medicine and CU Sports Medicine and Performance Center. “A herniation happens when the jelly inside pops out.”.

You may hear people using other terms like “bulging disc,” “ruptured disc,” or “slipped disc.” Technically, a bulging disc is just that: It’s when the jelly inside the donut is pushing against the side enough to bulge out from the vertebrae but isn’t leaking out. A ruptured or slipped disc refers to an actual herniation, where the doughnut cracks, allowing the gel-filled center to squeeze out.

Sources indicate that A bulging and/or herniated disc can cause pain by creating pressure on the nearby nerves. There’s some evidence that the leaked fluid from herniated discs also can cause chemical irritation and inflammation of the spinal nerve roots.

Again, it’s possible to have an asymptomatic herniated disc where you feel no pain. When you do have pain from a herniated disc, however, you’ll know it.

Sources indicate that pain from the herniated discs is sharp and radiating. Most cyclists experience herniated discs in the lower, lumbar back (we’ll get to why in a bit). So you may feel burning pain often known as sciatica that radiates from your lower back into your glutes and down one or both legs, sometimes even into your feet. You may feel pain similar to an electric shock when you stand or sit or walk. You may also feel radiating numbness, tingling, and/or weakness in your lower extremities.

So how does the jelly get out of the doughnut and start wreaking havoc on your spinal nerves? In a word: pressure. It can be extreme and sudden, like Jemison cranking on the cobbles. Or, in many instances, it can happen gradually over time, as was the case with Elsasser.

When your spine is in its generally straight, neutral position, the pressure from the top down is uniform on your discs, so the jelly inside those cushions is evenly distributed, Pruitt explains.

“When you bend forward, the jelly is pushed back, stressing the skin of that doughnut,” he says. “If you’re sitting all day, that jelly is pressing back there for eight hours. Now jump on a bike, and you add another two hours in an even more extreme position, pressing that jelly further and further, until—pop—it comes out.”.

Though herniation can happen anywhere in the spine, in cyclists it happens most frequently in the lumbar (low back) region close to the base of the spine, or the L5-S1, the bottom-most disc that sits right on top of your tailbone, because that’s where we bend the most, says Menachem Brodie, C.S.C.S., head coach at Human Vortex Training and USA Cycling expert coach.

“For many cyclists, the L5-S1 is where they’re getting their flexion, and the lumbar spine has about six degrees of movement,” Brodie states. So if you’re not hinging from the hips and keeping your spine within its safe, natural range, you’re pushing those limits. Keeping your spine under that kind of stress for prolonged periods of time pushes you closer to the failure point.

Along those lines, research indicates that riders with a lower handlebar position and greater flexion in that key lower back region were more likely to have low back pain. Though, importantly, the research also suggests that poor core strength and endurance could contribute to the spinal stress and low back pain in cyclists.

Of course, the bike isn’t the only place you can stress your spine. The gym can be another place riders put their spine under unhealthy stress, claims Dane DeLozier, D.P.T., the biomechanics lab director at and co-founder of Revo Physiotherapy and Sports Performance. Maintaining a stable, neutral spine is very crucial when resistance training, especially when doing big lifts like deadlifts and squats as well as under velocity like with kettlebell swings, DeLozier says.

According to recent reports, “When you have your spine under load, you want it to be neutral and very stabilized. You want to be hinging through your hips, not bending and extending your spine under load,” he says.

If you’re unsure of if you’re maintaining a neutral spine, DeLozier recommends setting up your phone and recording yourself (or having a friend video record you) so you can see if you are breaking or flexing under load.

According to recent reports, the good news is a 2020 scientific paper, “Slipped disc: Overview,” reports that about 90 percent of people will get relief from their pain and restricted movement within six weeks even if they receive no medical treatment. That’s because the body gets rid of part of the prolapsed tissue or it shifts position so that the nerves aren’t irritated anymore, according to the overview.

You can help that process along with physical therapy, DeLozier notes. “The vast majority of folks feel better and have a great outcome by doing mobility exercises for the hip and low back and decompression exercises for the spine.”.

The exercises you do depends on your individual situation, but your physical therapist may recommend mobility, stability, and core strengthening exercises such as:.

In a recent development, press Up: Lie facedown with your feet together, toes pointed, and your forearms on the floor palms. Pull your shoulder blades down and in towards your spine and press into forearms to lift your chest off of the floor, keeping your neck long and hips on the floor. If mobility allows, you can press up further by placing hands below your shoulders to come into an up-dog position. Hold for 3 to 5 seconds. Repeat about 15 times.

Hip Flexor Stretch: Kneel with the affected knee on the floor, tighten your glutes, and brace your abdominal muscles while keeping your back straight. Pressing hips forward. Hold this stretch for 30 seconds. Do 3 times.

Bird Dog: Get on your hands and knees with your palms flat on the floor, shoulder-width apart. Slowly raise and straighten your right leg and left arm at the same time. Keep your hips aligned with the torso and not tilted to one side. Hold for 10 seconds. Return to start. Repeat on the other side.

Recent findings suggest that cycling itself, when done with a healthy riding posture, can also be a great rehab tool to strengthen the discs and surrounding structures, Broadbent claims. In fact, a study done on high-volume road cyclists who rode nearly 100 miles a week for five or more years had beneficial adaptations to their discs and psoas (the biggest hip flexor muscle), which were beneficial for spinal health.

If you’re riding through your rehab, Brodie recommends “crocodile breathing” when you get off the bike. To do it, lie facedown with your forehead resting on the back of your hands and let your chest and hips sink into the floor. Inhale deeply into your belly, expanding your diaphragm for four slow counts. Pause for two seconds, then exhale for six slow counts.

Finally, while many herniated discs can be treated conservatively with physical therapy, some require injection therapy like nerve blocks, if the symptoms are severe, Broadbent states. In rare cases, spinal disc herniation can cause extreme pressure and swelling of the nerves at the end of the spinal cord causing a medical emergency known as cauda equina syndrome.

“If your bladder and bowels aren’t working properly, you have saddle numbness (off the bike as well), or you have sexual dysfunction such as unable to get an erection then you should seek urgent medical investigation,” Broadbent indicates.

Again, cycling can actually improve spinal strength and the health and hydration of your discs, says Broadbent.

Recent findings suggest that having a good bike position and the right saddle is key. “You want your spine in a healthy position that doesn’t strain those discs in your lower back,” Pruitt claims. If you ride a gravel or a mountain bike, you’re likely already in a slightly more upright, more neutral spine position, he says.

Industry observers note that an anatomical saddle will also allow you to put your weight on your perineum without putting harmful pressure on those sensitive tissues, so you’re able to reach the bars without bending too far and putting your spine in an unhealthy position. “Saddle technology improvements have really helped reduce degenerative disc disease,” he notes.

You also can protect your spine by doing core-strengthening exercises several times a week. Brodie recommends what are known as the “big three” exercises for spinal stability, developed by renowned back pain expert, Stuart McGill, Ph.D., Professor Emeritus of Spine Biomechanics at the University of Waterloo. These exercises stiffen the musculature throughout the core in a way that enhances stability in the spine.

How to do these exercises: The American Council of Exercise recommends performing three sets for each using a reverse pyramid rep/set scheme. Start with a higher number of repetitions for the first set, then decrease by 2 to 6 reps, then decrease by another 2 to 4 reps on the last set. So you might start with 8-6-4 reps and work your way up to 12-10-8 reps as you get stronger and build endurance. Hold each exercise for no more than 8 to 10 seconds.

It has been revealed that mcGill Curl-up: Lie on your back with one leg extended and the other leg bent, foot flat on the floor. Put your hands under your low back to maintain your natural arch. In one move, lift your head, shoulders, and chest off the floor, keeping your neck and back in the neutral position. Hold. Then slowly return to start. Do half a set. Then switch legs and complete the set.

Side Bridge: Lie on your right side, with your forearm on the floor and elbow underneath your shoulder. Bend your knees at a 90-degree angle. Place your left hand on the opposite shoulder for stability. Lift your hips off the floor so your body forms a straight line from your head to your knees. Hold. Then lower to the starting position and repeat to the other side. Work up to doing the move with your legs straight.

The Bird Dog: (As explained in the previous section).

You can make these exercises part of your warm-up, along with dynamic mobility moves before you get into your bigger lifts.

Off the bike, Brodie recommends practicing good spine hygiene by avoiding hunching forward when you sit and not sitting in a static position for prolonged periods of time, but rather shifting positions in your chair every 15 minutes and getting up, moving around, and doing a little standing stretch, extending your arms, reaching overhead and taking a deep breath every 60 to 90 minutes.

It has been revealed that finally, don’t overlook your mattress. A firm mattress with a pillow top will help support your spine while you sleep, Brodie states. “A lot of people overlook this and it can make a significant difference in your back health.”.

Can the Tour Be Pogačar-Proofed? The 2027 Tour de France Route Is Designed to Keep the Racing Close.

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it’s early November, which means the Halloween candy is on sale, the piles of leaves in my yard are getting harder to ignore, and the routes for the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France have finally been unveiled.
  • First, let’s address the Slovenian elephant in the room: There’s little anyone can do to defeat a healthy, in-form Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG), who will head into the 2027 Tour as the overwhelming favorite to take a record-breaking sixth overall victory.
  • Rather than create a race designed to defeat him, which right now doesn’t seem possible, they’ve laid out a course that could at least prevent the five-time champion from running away with it in the first week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s early November, which means the Halloween candy is on sale, the piles of leaves in my yard are getting harder to ignore, and the routes for the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France have finally been unveiled. After weeks of refreshing Tour rumor sites, here’s what stood out to me about the men’s route.

First, let’s address the Slovenian elephant in the room: There’s little anyone can do to defeat a healthy, in-form Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG), who will head into the 2027 Tour as the overwhelming favorite to take a record-breaking sixth overall victory. Certainly, the organizers seem to feel the same way.

Rather than create a race designed to defeat him, which right now doesn’t seem possible, they’ve laid out a course that could at least prevent the five-time champion from running away with it in the first week. The 2027 Tour packs more than 53,000 meters of elevation gain and 28 second-, first-, or hors catégorie climbs into its 21 stages. But there are only three summit finishes, and the first doesn’t arrive until the end of Stage 9, atop the Grand Colombier.

It has been revealed that that means fewer chances for Pogačar and his team to jump out to a huge early lead on the Tour’s general classification and then ride defensively, slowly wearing down the opposition until the final week. That’s when the Slovenian usually delivers the coup de grâce, adding a few more stage wins to his ever-growing tally.

Yes, there are a couple of punchy uphill finishes in the opening week, at the end of Stages 4 and 5, and Pogačar will do well on them. But the time gaps shouldn’t be huge, so I expect a tighter bunch of riders at the top of the GC heading into the first individual time trial on Stage 7.

Industry observers note that speaking of time trials, the 2027 Tour features 71 kilometers of them across Stages 7 and 16, the most we’ve seen since 2012. It’s hard not to see that as a nod to Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull–Bora–Hansgrohe), the four-time world time trial champion who finished second in the Tour this past July.

According to recent reports, if he can improve his preparation for this year’s Tour, and he’s only 26, Evenepoel could use those time trials to his advantage. The first might even give him a chance to give Pogačar a scare before the mountains arrive at the end of the opening week.

But waiting until Stage 9 for the first mountain stage doesn’t mean the opening week will be easy. A slew of long, tricky stages will be tough for one or two teams to control. And at least until the Stage 7 time trial, plenty of riders should be in contention to spend a day or two in yellow and willing to take a few risks and substantial swings to make it happen. That’s the downside of designing a route that attempts to delay the GC fireworks until the second week. More riders feel they have a chance to wear yellow, which can lead to more risk-taking and, unfortunately, the possibility of more crashes.

Throw in tight roads, punchy climbs and descents, some rain during the three opening stages in the United Kingdom, and perhaps a few days of crosswinds, and you’ve got the exact right mix to create unpredictable and downright chaotic racing.

If Pogačar is going to run away with another Tour, I expect we’ll know by the end of Stage 11, the final day in the Alps and the second of the race’s three summit finishes. If his rivals, including Evenepoel, Denmark’s Jonas Vingegaard (Visma–Lease a Bike), and France’s Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM Team), can somehow limit the damage on Stages 9, 10, and 11, we could have a much more compelling Tour than what we’re used to.

According to recent reports, A run of sprint and transitional stages follows before the final week, when the second time trial and two days in the Pyrenees await. With any luck, we’ll still have a GC battle worth watching by then.

Sources indicate that that’s what the organizers appear to be hoping for with this route. But given what we’ve seen from Pogačar and his UAE squad in recent Tours, I’m not sure it will happen. While the time trial kilometers seem to acknowledge Evenepoel as one of Pogačar’s greatest threats, I also see the route as a not-so-subtle gesture to Seixas, the young Frenchman many consider the rider most likely to be Pogačar's successor.

Seixas, now 20, raced his first Tour this past summer and finished fourth overall. The 2027 course should give him a chance to continue growing as a Tour contender without throwing him in at the deep end the way this year’s route did. The French would be thrilled to see him finish on the final podium, and with the Tour’s most intense stages broken into two- or three-day chunks, with time to recover and regroup in between, that kind of result looks well within his reach.

I’m also eager to see how two-time Tour champion Vingegaard tackles the race. Recent routes have forced Vingegaard and his Visma–Lease a Bike team to burn a lot of matches early, leaving them powerless when Pogačar and his UAE teammates throw down in the second and third weeks. The 2027 course should allow Vingegaard to ride a bit more under the radar, hopefully keeping him fresh for the Stage 7 time trial and the first summit finish on Stage 9. If all goes to initiative, the Dane could enter the third week ready to challenge Pogačar in a way we haven’t seen since Vingegaard won his second Tour in 2023.

As for specific stages, I’ve already marked a few as days I won’t want to miss.

The Tour begins in the United Kingdom with three stages that should generate some intense battles among sprinters and Classics riders. Of the three, Stage 3 looks like the hardest. Its 223 km route includes a slew of punchy climbs, making it a perfect day for riders like Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin–Premier Tech), Wout van Aert (Visma–Lease a Bike), and Tom Pidcock (Pinarello–Q36.5 Pro Cycling Team).

Then there’s Stage 10, a 171 km ride from Annecy to Sallanches that features six categorized climbs and previews the course used in August’s world championship road race. Coming right after the Tour’s second rest day and sandwiched between summit finishes on Stages 9 and 11, this should be an exciting and hard-to-predict day for the GC contenders.

Stage 14 takes the riders 199 km from Montpellier into the Cévennes, covering many of the roads immortalized in Tim Krabbé’s The Rider, one of the best cycling novels ever written. Seriously, if you’ve never read it, find a copy and enjoy! The stage ends on an airstrip just past the summit of the Côte de la Croix Neuve, a famous climb that always generates an exciting finish.

After taking a back seat in recent Tours, the Pyrenees close out the mountain racing in 2027, highlighted by Stage 18. The Tour’s “queen stage” runs 174 km from Pau to Saint-Lary-Soulan, with 5,400 meters of elevation gain and perhaps the two toughest climbs in the entire race: the Col du Tourmalet and a summit finish on the Col du Portet. If the race hasn’t been decided heading into Stage 18, it should be by the end, even with one relatively milder day in the Pyrenees still to come.

Industry observers note that and what about Stage 21? Maybe you heard the pre-announcement rumors that the organizers would skip the cobbled Côte de la Butte Montmartre. Thank goodness they proved false. Adding a few trips over the climb to the final stage in 2025 has proven to be one of the greatest innovations in Tour history, and I’m thrilled they kept it in for another year.

Overall, the 2027 men’s Tour stacks up like this: 3,479 kilometers (2,162 miles) spread over 21 stages, with seven flat stages, six hilly stages, six mountain stages, two individual time trials, and three rest days.

With about eight months to go before the riders hit the road in Edinburgh, a lot can still happen. Most of the top contenders haven’t even confirmed their 2027 programs, which means there’s a chance, however unlikely, that at least one of them might not participate.

Industry observers note that but as long as Pogačar is racing, the result, for better or worse, might be a foregone conclusion. And that’s not necessarily a bad thing. He is a once-in-a-lifetime talent, resetting the record books of the sport the way Eddy Merckx once did.

But as the saying goes: it’s the journey—not the destination—that matters here. Yes, we should enjoy speculating about who will and who won’t win the Tour de France—and how and when they manage to do it. But we can’t forget that the Tour de France offers at least 21 chances for something exciting and unexpected to unfold. Next year’s route might not prevent the inevitable, but it will certainly produce lots of great racing along the way. And I can’t wait.

#9878. Your First Gravel Ride Should Feel Like an Adventure—These 3 Tips Will Help You Enjoy It

Your First Gravel Ride Should Feel Like an Adventure—These 3 Tips Will Help You Enjoy It

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1489 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • The more riders I talk to, the more I see people switching over to gravel bikes.
  • In a recent development, over the last few years, I’ve focused more on gravel riding than any other discipline of cycling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

The more riders I talk to, the more I see people switching over to gravel bikes. I was leading a group ride for a shop in Upcoming Jersey and the group primarily consisted of road cyclists on their first gravel ride. The line of the day was, “this is so fun—it’s like being a kid on a bike.” Gravel is challenging, but it’s also a different type of fun once you get off paved roads.

In a recent development, over the last few years, I’ve focused more on gravel riding than any other discipline of cycling. My lunch rides typically end up being on the road and my strictly fun rides end up being on the mountain bike. But I’ve been gravitating more and more to the gravel bike because it can do a little bit of everything.

I’ve taken gravel bikes on everything from 100-mile road rides with 10,000 feet of climbing to rides on singletrack trails where we should have been on a hardtail mountain bike at a minimum. On bikepacking routes, gravel day rides, and family rides towing my kids in their bike trailer, the gravel bike has been my go-to rig.

Industry observers note that if you’re upcoming to the sport, or even just getting into the category of gravel riding, it's easy to feel like there’s a mountain of knowledge needed as a barrier to entry. Here we’ll break down the top gravel tips you need to know to find success in those first few rides and beyond.

When I ran a shop this was the first place I would start with folks who were gravel curious. The touchpoints on a bike are both where you contact the bike and where the bike touches the ground. The pieces of gear to focus on here are: chamois, gloves, saddle, bar tape, and tires.

According to recent reports, the chamois and gloves are the first two because they are the parts on your body that touch the bike. I don’t like to use gloves that are overly padded, but I do like gloves that have a good level of tackiness to help with staying gripped to the handlebars. This year I’ve been using the Most Days Full Finger Gloves from Handup for everything from century gravel group rides to hard gravel rides with plenty of singletrack. The chamois can be a little more subjective, but I almost always suggest going with chamois bibs over chamois shorts.

Sources indicate that bibs stay in place better than shorts and this is especially crucial from the movement you’re doing on a gravel ride. I’ve had plenty of people ask if they really need padded shorts for riding and the short answer is no. You can go riding with regular basketball shorts, but you’ll have a much better time riding with padded shorts or bibs. I like to compare it to riding a road bike on gravel. You can absolutely do that, and for a long time that’s what people did, but there’s a better way. My favorite pair are the Q36.5 Dottore Pro Bibs because they stay in place incredibly well and are comfortable from the first hour in the saddle to the 11th hour. The price point is a realistic hurdle for these Q36.5 bibs, but our Deputy Test Editor at Bicycling, Tara Seplavy, calls out this pair available on Amazon for just $40 in her roundup of cycling shorts.

I personally like a tape that has some tackiness while also offering a bit of cushion for some dampening after miles of chattering gravel. My favorite tape is the Lizard Skin DSP Ultra Bar Tape. It comes in a range of colors and thicknesses, but I usually go with the 2.7mm or 3.5mm for people riding gravel. If you want a little extra comfort over the miles size up to the 3.5mm.

When it comes to saddles this is much more subjective because everyone’s sit bones are different and your preferred saddle can change depending on your position on the bike. Personally I have different saddles on each of my bikes based on how I use that specific bike. The biggest note on saddles is to avoid going with something super wide and overly padded. This can be a desirable thing to reach for after you’ve developed a bit of soreness from your initial rides, but try to avoid the beach cruiser type of saddles. These can cause extra friction and that’s the last thing you want to add to your gravel ride.

Recent findings suggest that finally, we get to where the bike touches the ground—the tires. When someone is looking to add comfort and versatility to a gravel bike I usually recommend bumping up the tire size. Most bikes don’t come stock with the widest tire you can fit on the bike, so check the technical specifications for your bike to see how wide you can go. Some of my favorite gravel tires are the Pirelli Cinturato H tires and the Continental Dubnital tires for their versatility on a range of terrains.

In a recent development, this is a broad tip, but it is the most all-encompassing piece of advice I can give for gravel. Gravel riding burns more energy mile for mile and climb for climb compared to a road ride. Keep this in mind when you’re putting together your nutrition and hydration plan as well as when you’re building the route. It’s important to bring more calories than you think you need because you’ll likely be burning more calories compared to a road ride; it will take longer to get to the next refill stop compared to what you would expect, and those refuel spots are fewer and farther between on gravel roads and dirt trails compared to a road ride.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to setting up my route I always suggest riders have a way to navigate. When I got into gravel riding I used my phone for navigation with a handlebar mount on the bars. This worked initially, but because of the mud on some gravel routes, the possibility of falling, and how fast navigating on my phone killed the battery I quickly switched to a dedicated head unit. Head units that are capable of navigating reasonably well can range from a few hundred dollars to just shy of a thousand. At the moment I’m testing the COROS Dura 2 Solar and I love the fact that battery life can last for days of solid run time. A dedicated bike computer head unit is something that’s nice to have as you start to adventure, but if you currently have a smartwatch you can likely use that to navigate for now. It’s more convenient having the head unit in front of you for navigation compared to a smart watch. Lately I’ve been trying a few different watches from Garmin and COROS as a substitute for a bike computer and once I set up turn-by-turn notifications I’ve gotten used to navigating by the watch. Plus I can use the watch for other activities like runs, family hikes, and the occasional paddle.

Flat tires will eventually happen on a gravel ride. Step one is to bring a good flat kit with a reliable set of tire levers, a multitool (with a chain breaker), at least one tube, and a pump for inflation. I also typically bring a dollar bill as a backup for a tire boot in the event that I really blow out my tire. Ever since I had to use fallen leaves as a tire boot I always carry something to cover a large hole in the tire.

Recent findings suggest that step two is knowing how to use the tools you brought. Bringing a chain breaker tool or tire levers are great, but they won’t be much help if you aren’t able to figure out how to use them. When someone was buying a latest bike from me I used to encourage them to practice taking the wheels off the bike, tires off the wheels, tubes out of the tires, then putting it all back together. Getting some laps on this process from the comfort of your home will make the process feel much smoother when you’re trying to finish the flat fix on the side of the trail.

In a recent development, jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.
